#9548. CrowdStrike Makes AI Security Push With Blockbuster Zscaler Deal

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

CrowdStrike's $44 billion acquisition of Zscaler would unite endpoint protection and zero-trust network security to obtain greater control over AI agents.

CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire Zscaler for $43.9 billion in stock, combining endpoint protection and zero-trust network security to help enterprises control AI agents running across their systems.

The deal, announced Monday, aims to give chief information security officers (CISOs) a single supplier for security controls spanning endpoints where agents operate and the network connections used to reach applications and data.

The proposed transaction surpasses Google's $32 billion acquisition of Wiz, making it the largest announced cybersecurity acquisition on record. For customers, whether the companies can turn their existing integrations into unified enforcement while preserving support for competing products remains to be seen.

CrowdStrike co-founder and CEO George Kurtz said the proliferation of AI agents has changed the role of network security, making Zscaler's traffic inspection complementary to the Falcon platform's visibility into endpoints and cloud workloads.

Related:Microsoft Debuts Offensive, Defensive Security Tools for the AI Era

"The network used to connect people to places," Kurtz said during an investor call announcing the deal and discussing CrowdStrike's fiscal third-quarter results. "Now it connects agents to data."

CrowdStrike expects the transaction to close in the second half of fiscal 2028, subject to customary closing conditions. The companies will operate independently until then, according to CrowdStrike CFO Burt Podbere.

Bringing network and endpoint security into a common control plane makes sense even without the growth of AI agents, according to cybersecurity analyst Frank Dickson, founder of Dickson Research. Their increasing use makes the combination more compelling, he tells Dark Reading.

CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian discovers AI agents, governs their access, and protects them at runtime, Kurtz said. Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange provides inline inspection and access controls for traffic moving to applications and services. Combining those capabilities would connect what an agent does on a device with where it sends data, according to the two companies.

Kurtz described the planned integration with an example of an agent on a laptop pulling sensitive information and sending it to an unapproved AI model. Falcon would see the agent's activity on the device, while Zscaler would see the destination on the network.

"Together it will be one detection, one decision, and one kill switch that stops the agent on the device and cuts its path on the network," Kurtz said.

Related:Agentic Browsers Rewind Web Security by 20 Years

The companies already share 16 integrations, and customers send Zscaler data into CrowdStrike's Next-Gen SIEM. The combination would bring their telemetry together in that platform and use the expanded dataset to support CrowdStrike's security AI models, Kurtz said.

Zscaler founder, chairman, and CEO Jay Chaudhry said combining the companies will allow them to go beyond what they can accomplish through existing partner integrations, including coordinating policy enforcement across endpoints, cloud environments, and the network.

"Imagine being able to have a unified policy that can do all this stuff," Chaudhry said during the conference call.

Zscaler's network-centric architecture should make integrating the endpoint software less burdensome than it might seem because much of Zscaler's processing happens in its distributed network rather than on the device, Dickson says.

"The integration is going to be much lighter because much of the heavy lifting done by Zscaler is done in the network," he says.

According to Kurtz, CrowdStrike's next-generation endpoint sensor already has network traffic inspection and proxy capabilities that should help with integration. Asked during the call by Deutsche Bank analyst Brad Zelnick how the deal would affect CrowdStrike's single-software agent architecture, Kurtz reiterated that commitment without providing a delivery date for the combined agent.

Related:Agentic AI Challenges Progress in Confidential Computing

"The brand promise, single agent. That's not going to change," he said.

The CrowdStrike-Zscaler combination could "fundamentally change the competitiveness of the industry, 100%," Dickson says.

Microsoft has comparable breadth, he adds, but questions whether it could match the depth of the software giant's combined offerings. And it doesn't mean Palo Alto Networks, for example, needs another acquisition to respond. The vendor already has the technologies to compete, Dickson says, pointing particularly to its identity capabilities and its CyberArk deal.

Palo Alto Networks is also pursuing a different route into enterprise AI. Its Nov. 18 agreement to acquire Applied Compute for $4.5 billion in stock would extend its reach into training and deploying open-weight AI models. While CrowdStrike is emphasizing controls over where agents run and communicate, Palo Alto is moving further into the infrastructure used to build and operate enterprise AI.

"They're changing the terms of competition away from functionality to trust," Dickson says of Palo Alto's approach.

Dickson also points to Cisco's expansion in identity, underscoring the wider competition to connect identity with security enforcement.

For other security vendors, the Zscaler acquisition increases the importance of partnerships and differentiation by industry or customer size, Dickson says. Microsoft's broad security portfolio already required that approach; the CrowdStrike-Zscaler combination would add another large platform competitor, he notes.

"You need as many friends as you can, and then niche as hard as you can," Dickson says.

For CISOs, the competitive shift also raises the question about whether a broader platform can simplify security operations without limiting product choice.

After closing, CrowdStrike intends to bring Zscaler's offerings into Falcon Flex, allowing customers to expand across both portfolios through the same subscription model. CrowdStrike's Podbere said cross-selling and broader adoption would help generate approximately $1 billion in annualized revenue savings within 30 months after closing.

Deutsche Bank's Zelnick asked what the transaction would mean for customers that want another endpoint or secure access service edge (SASE) provider. Kurtz emphasized the single-agent strategy rather than detailing how those mixed-vendor deployments would work.

Separately, responding to a question about vendor lock-in, Kurtz said CrowdStrike would continue working with outside technologies and accepting data from other vendors.

Coexistence with competing network security products is already common, Dickson says, and he does not see the acquisition itself as a reason for those customers to change course. Deeper integration could make adding Zscaler more attractive to existing CrowdStrike customers, he says.

Despite his enthusiasm, Dickson says the CrowdStrike-Zscaler combination needs stronger identity capabilities to deliver on its AI-agent security ambitions. Discovering an agent and inspecting its traffic are not the same as establishing its identity and determining precisely what it is authorized to do.

Agents need a registry, authentication tied to their identities, and fine-grained authorization, Dickson says, though he questions whether either company's current portfolio fully provides that combination of capabilities.

CrowdStrike is working to address that area. During the investor Q&A, Kurtz said the company expects to introduce an agent identity provider around January, with controls intended to provide just-in-time access and zero standing privileges across human, machine, and agent identities.

The challenge is expanding as employees outside software development gain the ability to build agents, Dickson says. Security teams must contend not only with more agents but also with greater autonomy and creators who may lack experience building secure applications.

Jeffrey Schwartz is a New York–based freelance writer specializing in information security and enterprise IT. Jeff has contributed to Dark Reading since 2022 and has written for Channel Futures for over five years. Before launching his freelance career, he was an editor at 1105 Media, where he served as editor-in-chief of Redmond magazine and contributed to its sister publications, including Redmond Channel Partner, Application Development Trends, and Virtualization Review.

Previously, Jeff held editorial roles at CMP Media’s CommunicationsWeek, InternetWeek, and VARBusiness. #9547. Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#9546. Windows Retail vs. OEM vs. Volume Licenses: What's the Difference?

I run KRBKeys, a small Windows and Office key shop. Most of my day is fixing activation errors, so I write up what actually works.

I run KRBKeys, a small Windows and Office key shop. Most of my day is fixing activation errors, so I write up what actually works.

I run KRBKeys, a small Windows and Office key shop. Most of my day is fixing activation errors, so I write up what actually works.

I run a small shop that sells Windows and Office licenses, and the question I answer most isn't about price. It's "why did my key stop working?" Nine times out of ten the answer comes down to which of the three license channels the key belongs to. They all install the exact same Windows, but the rules attached to them are very different.

Retail is the one you buy for yourself. It isn't tied to a specific machine, so when you replace your PC you can deactivate it on the old one and activate it on the new one. One PC at a time, but it moves with you. It also comes with direct support from Microsoft.

OEM is what ships on a laptop or a prebuilt desktop. The license locks to the first motherboard it activates on and stays there for life. That's fine until the board dies or you build a new PC, at which point the old license can't follow you. A lot of "my Windows suddenly isn't activated" emails start with a motherboard swap on an OEM machine.

Volume licensing is for companies. A business buys a pool of activations and either hands out a multiple activation key or runs its own activation server, called KMS. Those keys were never meant for one person at home. When one ends up sold to a consumer it might work for a while, then fail months later with 0xC004C060 or 0xC004F074 once the key is blocked or the server stops answering.

Last week someone wrote to me after swapping a dead motherboard. Same case, same drive, same Windows install, but suddenly the "Activate Windows" watermark was back. He'd tried the troubleshooter, picked "I changed hardware on this device recently", and got told there were no devices linked to his account.

It turned out his Windows had come preinstalled on the PC, so it was an OEM license tied to the old board. Nothing he clicked was ever going to move it. If he'd had a retail key, entering it again would have taken thirty seconds. Same Windows, same symptoms, completely different outcome, and the only thing that changed was the license channel.

I see the reverse too. People who bought a retail key years ago assume they need a new one for their new PC, when they could have just moved the old one over.

Here's the short version I give customers:

One more thing that trips people up: the edition has to match. A Home key won't activate Pro, and a Pro key won't activate Home. If you clean-install and pick the wrong edition during setup, even a perfectly valid key gets rejected.

Open Command Prompt as administrator and run slmgr /dli. The Description line ends in RETAIL, OEM or VOLUME, and the Name line tells you the edition. If License Status says Notification instead of Licensed, Windows isn't activated.

If you'd rather not use the command line, go to Settings > System > Activation. It won't show the channel, but it will tell you whether Windows is activated and whether the license is linked to your Microsoft account. Linking it is worth doing either way, because it makes reactivating after a hardware change much easier.

Since this is the part that costs people money, a few things I'd always look at:

If you expect to upgrade or rebuild your PC, a retail license is worth having because it survives the hardware change. If your machine came with Windows preinstalled, treat that license as part of the computer. And if a deal on a key looks too good to be true, check the channel before you count on it lasting.

I run KRBKeys, a small Windows and Office key shop. Most of my day is fixing activation errors, so I write up what actually works.

#9545. Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites

At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

This entry was posted on Tuesday 17th of November 2026 09:52 PM

Using an A/B testing platform as the delivery mechanism is a genuinely uncomfortable escalation: the tool that decides which visitors see which experience was never modeled as a malware distribution channel, so none of the usual detections fire. The operational discipline angle is what stands out – attackers versioning and measuring payloads like product features means defenders need the same rigor about what their third-party tags are allowed to change. Supply-chain reviews for marketing stacks rarely get the scrutiny payments or auth integrations do; this will change that.

#9544. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

#9543. Industrial Serial Gateways Broadcast That They're Insecure

Critical OT access devices will often tell you, and anyone else, whether they're protected by authentication — and many aren't.

Internet scans indicate that some substantial fraction of serial device servers deployed at operational technology (OT) sites worldwide not only lack authentication but also broadcast the fact publicly.

We all have a friend or a family member who's deeply insecure, and it's obvious as soon as they start talking. The same can be said of serial-to-IP gateways. Recently, Adrian Cheek, senior cybercrime researcher for Flare, probed the wider Internet for these sorts of devices, finding that a substantial chunk of them are discoverable. Worse, they often responded to straightforward requests by saying whether they were or were not protected by authentication — and many were not.

An insecure serial-to-IP gateway is a serious risk to anyone downstream of it. These devices are responsible for translating information between the Internet and industrial machinery. So in a cyberattack, a reachable and unauthenticated one can inadvertently translate an Internet-based threat into one that affects major, safety-critical machines.

Related:How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

Using a specific vendor's UDP discovery service, rather than probing all vendors' devices, Cheek found 2,474 serial-to-IP gateways exposed on the Web. They seemed to map to real devices rather than honeypots, with half of them located in Russia.

For some reason, in response to the researcher's unsolicited probes, around half of the devices — 1,265 — proffered their authentication status. Of those that did, 973 reported that authentication was disabled. In other words, 39.3% of all Internet-exposed gateways visibly lacked authentication, and among those whose status could be gleaned, that figure was 77%.

"These devices ship with authentication off. An integrator sets one up on a bench, gets the meter or the drive or the Remote Terminal Unit (RTU) talking to the SCADA host, and moves on to the next site," Cheek laments. "The device then does one job for 10 or 15 years, and nobody logs into it again. In many cases, the operator doesn't even know it exists because it went in as part of someone else's equipment."

There are also understandable, if not entirely justifiable, reasons why operators fail to conceal and lock down their serial device servers. Cheek cites a multitude of reasons, including that enabling such security features can break software on the host side.

"Older SCADA packages and virtual serial port drivers may not support the secured modes, so an operator who switches them on can lose the link to the field," he says. "Then someone has to drive to an unstaffed site to fix it. Firmware updates carry the same risk at a remote site with no spare on hand. People who have been burned by that once are slow to touch a working device again."

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

Still, an exposed, unauthenticated serial gateway is a welcome mat for bad actors. Not only does it give arbitrary actors entry into sensitive OT systems and eliminate the need to exploit any kind of vulnerabilities, it also allows attackers to use the vendor's own supplied tools, which could blend malicious activity in with normal IT-OT traffic.

Cheek made special mention of the risk to mobile network operators and, even more specifically, private access point name (APN) service providers. Last year's Polish power grid attack used a private APN to pivot from a wind farm's network to the power plant where the attackers ultimately shut down a steam turbine, water treatment system, and seven serial-to-IP devices. According to Flare, 322 of the 2,474 discovered devices in the study lived in address space associated with known mobile network operators in Europe and the Middle East.

OT operators can begin to secure their OT access layer by first doing an inventory of the devices they're running. "For every cellular unit, find out what plan the SIM is on and whether it gets a public address. Then ask your carrier in writing whether devices on your private network can reach each other or devices belonging to other customers," Cheek notes. "Don't assume the managed product isolates them. In the Polish incident, that missing isolation is what let the attacker move between two unrelated organizations."

Related:Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Next, he advises, "Lock down the data ports as well as the login. Most of these devices let you restrict which IP addresses can open a connection. Configure them so only the SCADA host can reach the serial ports and only an engineering workstation can reach the management interface. Switch off the services you don't use, which on most units means the discovery service, Telnet, older SNMP, and often the Web interface. Remove SSH and Telnet entirely from anything that faces the carrier network," and plop a strict firewall between the gateway and control network.

There are also general practices organizations can put in place, like ensuring that the next time they purchase serial device servers, a person or team is assigned to be responsible for the devices, and that they have necessary credentials, configuration, and network details from system integrators.

At the end of the day, though, nothing compares to preventing an attacker's ability to find and speak to a device in the first place.

"Even a fully patched gateway with authentication on is usually connected to equipment on the serial side that has no security of its own," Cheek points out. "A meter, a drive, or an RTU will accept any correctly formed command that reaches it. So the useful question is who can reach the gateway at all, because whoever can reach it gets whatever is behind it. Authentication and patching both matter, but restricting what can reach the gateway does more good than either."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9542. Debugging OAuth Redirect Loops Caused by Oversized HTTP Cookies

Last week, we spent almost four hours tracking down a login bug that made zero sense on paper.

Our dashboard users signing in with Google or Discord were getting thrown into an infinite redirect loop. They would hit sign in, pick their Google account, authorize it, watch the screen flash for a second, and then land right back on the empty login form.

No error message. No red toast. No failed requests in Chrome's network tab. Nothing in the console either.

Meanwhile, plain old email-and-password logins worked perfectly. Same database, same API server, same users. If an account logged in with a password, it went straight to the dashboard. If that exact same account clicked "Sign in with Google", it got kicked right back to square one.

To explain why this happened, you have to look at how we split our frontend and backend. The client dashboard runs on one subdomain, and the core API runs on another.

When someone signs in with an email and password, the frontend just fires an asynchronous POST request to our auth endpoint. The API checks the credentials, returns a 200 with the user profile and session data right in the JSON response body, and the frontend JavaScript saves that into localStorage and routes to the dashboard.

OAuth can't do that because the initial handoff isn't an in-page fetch request. The user gets bounced to Google's consent screen on google.com, and Google bounces them back to our API callback route on our API subdomain.

During initial development, this worked every single time. We created test accounts, clicked through OAuth, and landed on the dashboard without an issue.

The bug only showed up when we started testing with older, heavily used accounts.

When one of us tried to log in with an account we had been using for weeks across multiple laptops and phones, the redirect loop kicked in immediately.

But we checked our flags, and we were already using SameSite=Lax, Secure, and an explicit parent domain. That should have been completely fine under modern browser specs.

Then we thought we might have a race condition in our frontend code. We had an event listener in the login view listening for window focus events to catch popups, so we wondered if the tab was gaining focus mid-redirect and wiping state.

We removed that listener, tested again, and the loop was still there.

Eventually we opened Chrome DevTools, turned on "Preserve log" in the Network tab, and watched the whole redirect chain step by step.

That user record had an array called sessions. Every time a user logged in, our database pushed an entry tracking their device, IP, user-agent string, and login time.

On a brand new test account with one session, that whole JSON object was around 300 bytes. It easily fit inside the 4KB limit. But on our personal accounts, which had logged in dozens of times during testing, that session array had 10 or 15 items. The raw JSON alone grew to about 2.6KB.

Every quote turns into %22. Every bracket turns into %7B or %7D. Every colon turns into %3A. Every comma turns into %2C.

In practice, percent-encoding regular JSON inflates the byte size by about 2.4 times.

Email and password login never had this problem because the user data returned in the HTTP response body has no 4KB limit. The frontend read the body, saved it to localStorage, and navigated cleanly.

Third, we updated our frontend auth hook to check the URL query parameters on mount. If it sees auth_success=true, it immediately fires a background fetch request to our user profile endpoint to pull the full user object over a normal HTTP body.

As soon as that request finishes and localStorage is updated, the frontend calls window.history.replaceState to scrub the query parameters out of the URL bar so the user never sees them.

The biggest lesson for us was just how quiet browser networking failures can be.

If your backend throws a 500 or your React code throws an exception, you get an immediate alert or a red error in your console.

#9541. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

#9540. 'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

Attackers could have disrupted traveler entry into Nigeria, Ethiopia, Zambia, Sri Lanka, Fiji, and Ghana via several vulnerabilities in their online visa and immigration systems.

Imagine trying to enter a country you've always wanted to visit, only to find yourself not only denied entry but potentially arrested because you've mistakenly ended up on a list of known terrorists.

This is one of several scenarios that could have unfolded if attackers had exploited flaws that independent security researcher Eaton Zveare discovered in the online passport and border-control systems of several countries: Nigeria, Ethiopia, Fiji, Zambia, Sri Lanka, and Ghana.

Though specific to each system, the flaws generally allowed unauthorized access to millions of travelers' sensitive visa and passport data — potentially including biometric information such as fingerprints — and, in some cases, even granted access to administrative functions that could be used to approve or deny entry into a country.

Specifically, Zveare discovered critical API vulnerabilities, including broken object-level authorization (BOLA), broken function-level authorization (BFLA), and missing authentication, in online systems these countries use to process visa applications and authorize travelers to enter.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Many of the systems were built by third-party contractors with varying levels of expertise, which likely contributed to the relatively simple and easily avoidable security gaps, Zveare tells Dark Reading. In Nigeria's case, an over-reliance on AI to build the systems may also have introduced flaws into the code.

"I think they've gotten on the AI hype train, and they've kind of used it to build their border control a little bit," he says.

Taken together, the vulnerabilities — which should never exist in "the systems that are vital to national security" — highlight a broader failure to secure critical national infrastructure, potentially with significant consequences for people traveling to these countries, Zveare says.

"The tip of the iceberg is not only viewing all the people who ever applied for these visas and passports, but actually being able to approve or deny applications that are currently coming in," he says, describing the potential for bad actors to exploit the flaws.

Zveare describes the level of access the flaws could provide as "God mode at the border" — also the title of a session he will lead at Black Hat Europe next month about his findings. By exploiting the vulnerabilities, attackers could effectively "have the master key to these countries and their borders," potentially threatening the safety of both citizens and people entering the country. Zveare will disclose the details of the flaws during his session, which is scheduled for Dec. 10.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

The discovery began almost by accident, when Zveare searched Microsoft Bing for the phrase "admin panel" about a year ago. One of the results led him to a private back-end portal belonging to Nigeria.

After investigating the portal, Zveare uncovered security flaws that gave him access to sensitive immigration systems. Intrigued by what he had found, he began looking for similar systems in other countries, focusing on online passport-control and visa platforms built using modern Web technologies such as Angular and React.

His search eventually led him to five more countries, where he discovered a range of vulnerabilities, including missing authentication and broken access controls — the kinds of common Web flaws that you often see but ones that "you just can't have in critical systems like this," Zveare tells Dark Reading.

In Nigeria alone, Zveare identified roughly a dozen vulnerabilities, while the other countries had several each. He went on to develop exploits to demonstrate how the flaws could allow an attacker not only to view sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to visa applicants, but also to access administrative functions that could determine whether someone was granted entry into a country.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

The potential consequences extend well beyond disrupted travel plans and compromised personal information, Zveare says. One worst-case scenario would involve an attacker identifying a high-level executive or other person of interest who might be targeted for kidnapping or assassination, then accessing their travel itinerary, hotel information, and other details that could be used to track their movements.

"You would know exactly when they land, where they are staying, and how long they're staying," Zveare says. "I'm sure you can imagine what bad people could do with that info."

Because the systems were spread across multiple foreign countries, many of which rely on outside companies to build their online infrastructure, identifying the parties responsible for fixing the vulnerabilities proved trickier than a typical bug disclosure, Zveare says.

"So all these countries have their computer emergency response teams (CERTs)," he tells Dark Reading. "Unfortunately, a lot of them did not respond."

One country whose response was particularly strong was also the one whose systems had the most problems: Nigeria, which moved quickly to resolve the vulnerabilities. Its response team had "a generally excellent response," Zveare says.

Indeed, Nigeria is emerging as "the big tech hub of Africa," and he expected its authorities to be relatively on top of these issues, he says.

When a country's CERT failed to respond, Zveare had to dig deeper to identify the independent contractor that had built the system and contact the company directly. In many cases, this proved to be the quickest route to remediation.

Overall, response times ranged from a few days to more than six months. By now, however, "everything is pretty much fixed," he says.

While Zveare says all the contractors he contacted were helpful and responsive in addressing the vulnerabilities, their security practices may have contributed to the problems in the first place.

"[The contractors] might have come in at the lowest bid, and that's what the country went with," Zveare says. "I feel as though, with how simple some of these flaws were, they might not have the most sophisticated security reviews."

One quick test Zveare uses when assessing a Web API is to look for an administrative endpoint that retrieves a list of all users. "So I'll uncover that, and I'll just copy that endpoint into my browser and see what happens."

In the case of the vulnerable border-control systems, "a lot of the time, they would just return the entire users list because they don't check for the authentication token," he says.

The problems went beyond improper token handling, however. In some cases, authentication tokens were missing altogether, meaning sensitive endpoints could be accessed without the required authentication.

This lack of fundamental Web security points to a broader failure of oversight by national authorities when selecting the contractors entrusted with building and maintaining their systems, Zveare says. For infrastructure as sensitive as border control systems, that lack of scrutiny is not only unacceptable but potentially dangerous.

"You have to properly vet these contractors because you're giving your nation's security to them," Zveare says. "And if they don't know basic Web security, you're going to have a bad time."

#9539. Ginger VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?


Ginger VS Grammarly: When it comes to grammar checkers, Ginger and Grammarly are two of the most popular choices on the market. This article aims to highlight the specifics of each one so that you can make a more informed decision about the one you'll use.

What is Grammarly?

If you are a writer, you must have heard of  Grammarly before. Grammarly has over 10M users across the globe, it's probably the most popular AI writing enhancement tool, without a doubt. That's why there's a high chance that you already know about Grammarly.

But today we are going to do a comparison between Ginger and Grammarly, So let's define Grammarly here. Like Ginger, Grammarly is an AI writing assistant that checks for grammatical errors, spellings, and punctuation. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

While the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

Features of Grammarly

  • Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a personal dictionary 
  • Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Understand inconsistencies. 
  • Detect unclear structure. 
  • Detect Plagiarism.
  • Explore overuse of words and wordiness. 
  • Get to know about the improper tones. 
  • Discover the insensitive language aligns with your intent, audience, style, emotion, and more.


What is Ginger

 Ginger is a writing enhancement tool that not only catches typos and grammatical mistakes but also suggests content improvements. As you type, it picks up on errors then shows you what’s wrong, and suggests a fix. It also provides you with synonyms and definitions of words and allows you to translate your text into dozens of languages.


Ginger Software: Features & Benefits

  • Ginger's software helps you identify and correct common grammatical mistakes, such as consecutive nouns, or contextual spelling correction.
  • The sentence rephrasing feature can help you convey your meaning perfectly.
  • Ginger acts like a personal coach that helps you practice certain exercises based on your mistakes.
  • The dictionary feature helps users understand the meanings of words.

In addition, the program provides a text reader, so you can gauge your writing’s conversational tone.


Ginger vs Grammarly

Grammarly and Ginger are two popular grammar checker software brands that help you to become a better writer. But if you’re undecided about which software to use, consider these differences:

  • Grammarly only supports the English language while Ginger supports 40+ languages.
  • Grammarly offers a wordiness feature while Ginger lacks a Wordiness feature.
  • Grammarly shows an accuracy score while Ginger lacks an accuracy score feature.
  • Grammarly has a plagiarism checker while ginger doesn't have such a feature.
  • Grammarly can recognize an incorrect use of numbers while Ginger can’t recognize an incorrect use of numbers.
  • Grammarly and Ginger both have mobile apps.
  • Ginger and Grammarly offer monthly, quarterly, and annual plans.
  • Grammarly allows you to check uploaded documents. while Ginger doesn't check uploaded documents.
  • Grammarly Offers a tone suggestion feature while Ginger doesn't offer a tone suggestion feature.
  • Ginger helps to translate documents into 40+ languages while Grammarly doesn't have a translation feature.
  • Ginger Offers text to speech features while Grammarly doesn't have such features.


Grammarly Score: 7/10

Ginger:4/10

So Grammarly  wins here.

Ginger VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • Ginger offers a Premium subscription for 13.99$/month. it comes at $11.19/month for quarterly and $7.49/month for an annual subscription with 40$ off.
  • On the other hand,  Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly, and $12/month for an annual subscription.

For companies with three or more employees, the Business plan costs $12.50/month for each member of your team. 

Ginger Wins Here

Ginger vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons


Grammarly Pros

  • Offers  free version
  • All-in-one tool (grammar checker + spell checker + punctuation checker)
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Style checker (paid version)

  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Free mobile apps 
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Can upload and download documents


Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy

Ginger Pros

  • Offers free version
  • All-in-one tool (grammar checker + spell checker + punctuation checker)
  • Affordable Subscription plans (Additionals discounts are available)
  • Active and passive voice changer
  • Translates documents in 40+ languages

  • Browser extension available

Ginger Cons

  • Mobile apps aren't free
  • Limited monthly corrections for free users
  • No style checker
  • No plagiarism checker
  • Not as user-friendly as Grammarly
  • You are unable to upload or download documents; however, you may copy and paste files as needed.
  • Doesn't offer a free trial


Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

While both writing assistants are fantastic in their ways, you need to choose the one you want. 

For example, go for Grammarly if you want a plagiarism tool included. 

Choose Ginger if you want to write in languages other than English. I will to the differences for you in order to make the distinctions clearer.

  • Grammarly offers a plagiarism checking tool
  • Ginger provides text to speech tool

#9538. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.
