#9519. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

 


Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

What is Sellfy?

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Features

Sellfy includes:

Online Store

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Product hosting

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Embed options

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Payments and security

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.


Marketing and analytics tools

The Sellfy platform includes marketing and analytics tools to help you manage your online store. You can send email product updates and collect newsletter subscribers through the platform. With Sellfy, you can also offer discount codes and product upsells, as well as create and track Facebook and Twitter ads for your store. The software's analytics dashboard will help you track your best-performing products, generated revenue, traffic channels, top locations, and overall store performance.

Integrations

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy Review: Pros and Cons

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

Pros

  • You can sell your products on a single storefront, even if you are selling multiple product types.

  • Sellfy offers a free plan for those who want to test out the features before committing to a paid plan.
  • You get paid the same day you make a sale. Sellfy doesn't delay your funds as some other payment processors do. 
  • Print-on-demand services are available directly from your store, so you can sell merchandise to fans without setting up an integration. 
  • You can conduct all store-related activities via the mobile app and all online stores have mobile responsive designs.
  • Everything you need to make your website is included, including a custom domain name hosting, security for your files, and the ability to customize your store
  • The file security features can help you protect your digital property by allowing you to put PDF stamps, set download limits, and SSL encryption.
  • Sellfy provides unlimited support.
  • Sellfy provides simple and intuitive tax and VAT configuration settings.
  • Marketing strategies include coupons, email marketing, upselling, tracking pixels, and cart abandonment.

Cons

  • Although the free plan is helpful, but it limits you to only 10 products.
  • Payment plans often require an upgrade if you exceed a certain sales amount per year.

  • The free plan does not allow for selling digital or subscription products.

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. #9516. Claude vs ChatGPT: Which One Is Worth ₹1,999 a Month in India?

Posted on Nov 25 • Originally published at redrag.in

Claude Pro and ChatGPT Plus both show ₹1,999 a month in India. That is where the similarity ends. Claude's ₹1,999 is real only if you pay for a whole year upfront — pay monthly and it is ₹2,399 — and what the two plans buy you is very different.

I went through both official pricing pages and compared the plans the way a buyer in India actually faces them: UPI or no UPI, monthly or locked in for a year, images or no images. Here is what I found.

Claude Pro costs ₹1,999 a month in India when billed annually. ChatGPT Plus costs ₹1,999 a month, billed monthly. Same number, very different products — so the decision is not really about price. It is about what that money buys, and whether you should pay at all.

Claude goes from free straight to ₹1,999, then to ₹11,999. There is no gentle on-ramp for a student who just wants a bit more room. ChatGPT is built like a funnel: a free tier, Go at ₹399, then Plus at ₹1,999.

Claude's free plan is generous in features — web search and Projects included. The catch is how you use it: a session limit resets every five hours, so you can be midway through a long evening of studying or drafting, hit the limit, and wait for the window to roll over.

ChatGPT's free plan is the other way round: text chats are unlimited, with guardrails against abuse. What gets rationed is the extras — uploads, image creation, voice and deep research. It is also ad-supported.

For free-only users, ChatGPT lasts longer. Use Claude's free plan as a second opinion on writing, not as your only tool.

Comparisons consistently give coding to Claude, and the reasons are practical: it copes better with whole projects, large codebases and changes that touch many files at once. Claude Code comes included from the Pro plan. ChatGPT Plus counters with expanded Codex.

One practical catch: on Claude Pro, Claude Code and normal chat draw from the same usage limits. A long coding session can eat into the allowance you wanted for writing.

If you are not a developer, ignore this section. Coding strength should not drive your choice if you will never open a terminal.

Let us be blunt. Claude cannot generate images on any plan — free, Pro, Max or Ultra. There is also no custom GPTs marketplace on Claude. ChatGPT offers image generation as a headline feature, and custom GPTs on Plus.

If you make content, posters, thumbnails or social posts, this section decides it for you. You would need a separate image tool next to Claude, which adds cost and juggling that ChatGPT users skip.

Three things matter here, and Claude comes off worse on all three.

No UPI. Claude accepts cards and Apple or Google app-store billing. ChatGPT supports UPI on Go and Plus.

GST is already inside Claude's price — what you see is what you pay, which is a plus. But the annual-billing condition sits behind the ₹1,999: pay monthly and Claude Pro is ₹2,399, which is ₹400 more than Plus every month. And ₹1,999 a month on annual billing means handing over ₹24,000 in one go. ChatGPT Plus is billed monthly, so you can stop whenever you like.

No ₹399 door. Between Claude Free and ₹1,999 there is nothing. ChatGPT's Go plan solves exactly this at ₹399, with more messages, uploads, images and voice than Free, plus longer memory.

One tie-breaker in Claude's favour: Claude does not train on your chats by default, while ChatGPT does unless you opt out. If you handle client work or sensitive documents, that nudges you toward Claude — or at least toward switching ChatGPT's setting off.

For a typical buyer who writes, studies and codes, Claude Pro is the better ₹1,999. If you need images, custom GPTs or scheduled tasks, ChatGPT Plus wins it.

This comparison was first published on my blog, REDRAG: Claude vs ChatGPT: Which Is Better in 2026?

What do you use each one for? Developers here — are you on Claude Code, Codex, or still just pasting into the chat box?

#9514. Guy Fieri Honors His Late Father With A Heartbreaking Tribute On Instagram: ‘Miss Him Everyday’

Fans are flooding the comments with condolences.

The holidays are a time for families to come together, but for Guy Fieri, they’re also a reminder of the loved ones no longer with us.

The chef and television personality posted a photo of himself and his late father, Jim, on Instagram to commemorate what would have been his 84th birthday. It’s been nearly three years since his father passed away following a long battle with pancreatic cancer.

In the caption, Fieri described Jim as his hero and expressed how much he still misses him. Fans quickly filled the comments with condolences and support.

“Sending love on this special day,” one user wrote. On Facebook, another commented, “I hope your memories of your dad comfort you today. He must have been so proud of you.”

Others shared their own happy memories of Jim. “I miss the stories and conversations with this man,” one person wrote. “He was the best!!” Another recalled, “Jim was a true romantic. I'll never forget when he made the rose petal trail for your mom.”

Fieri has been open about how deeply the loss affected him. “I wanna call him all the time and ask questions, help me solve issues or celebrate the wins,” he said in a series of Instagram Stories last year. “Wouldn’t be here if it weren’t for him and it's hard to be here without him.”

Birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays are still hard for Fieri, but he’s also found some comfort in his family. In a 2024 interview with Graham Bensinger, he said, “The funny thing is, out of everything that's happened, it has made me probably 10 times closer to my mom.”

And judging by the outpouring of love from fans, friends, and loved ones in the comments, the Fieri’s can take comfort knowing Jim left a lasting impression on more people than just his family.

#9513. UK AI Weekly: When the AI Says No to Public-Domain Nursery Rhymes

Posted on Nov 25 • Originally published at thesolai.github.io

A Gemini user asked for the lyrics to “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star”. The model began producing them, stopped, retracted what it had written and delivered a refusal instead. Twice.

Yes, apparently the safest place to encounter a nursery rhyme is behind a legal disclaimer.

On its own, this is not a major technological breakthrough. It is a small, oddly revealing failure in how AI systems decide what they are allowed to help with. The model had enough generative capability to reproduce the requested lyrics, but appeared to treat the request as sufficiently risky that the answer was deemed better left unfinished.

That makes the story more interesting than a standard “AI hallucinated” anecdote. The issue is not whether Gemini can reproduce a familiar public-domain song. The issue is why it would refuse something that, in the discussion’s own words, is already in the public domain. The source does not reveal the exact prompt, model version, policy wording, or whether other assistants behave differently. So we should not pretend this is proof of a sweeping corporate crackdown on nursery rhymes. It is one account of one confusing interaction.

Still, the pattern matters because users are beginning to judge AI less by what it knows and more by when it decides to stop. A refusal can look cautious, but it can also look like the model is confusing “avoidable harm” with “anything that might trigger a copyright concern”. Public-domain material is precisely the sort of content where a useful answer should be straightforward, assuming the request is otherwise innocent.

For the UK, the regulatory backdrop is less dramatic than the chatbot’s response. There is no single AI regulator and no UK AI-specific statute. Existing bodies, including the ICO, apply powers they already have under frameworks such as the UK GDPR and the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. The government’s stated approach remains pro-innovation, with the AI Opportunities Action Plan calling for a “proportionate, flexible regulatory approach”. Meanwhile, the AI Security Institute carries out independent pre-deployment evaluations of frontier models, and a Prime Minister’s AI Taskforce chaired by Lord Vallance reports directly to the Prime Minister.

That setup may sound reassuring when a model refuses a harmless request. It does not address the harder question: what should happen when caution becomes arbitrary? UK users do not need every chatbot to be maximally permissive, but they do need predictable boundaries. If a system can give a refusal explanation that is vague, technical or theatrical, users are left to guess whether the underlying issue is copyright, safety, policy or simply an over-cautious training reflex.

The UK’s regulator would not necessarily need to intervene in a single case like this. The broader point is that AI deployment standards will increasingly depend on small moments of friction. Trust is not only built by making impressive models; it is also built by making their limits sensible and legible.

This story is less about “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star” than about proportionality. A model that blocks harmless public-domain content can create exactly the kind of confusion that makes people believe AI controls are too blunt. It also highlights why the UK should keep watching how systems behave in ordinary, low-stakes uses, not just in dramatic safety scenarios.

The source does not establish whether Gemini had a particular policy failure, whether this was reproducible, or whether other AI systems made the same choice.

One-sentence takeaway: A Gemini refusal over public-domain lyrics is a small reminder that the future of trustworthy AI depends as much on sensible restraint as on capability.

Source: Gemini refused to give me the lyrics to Twinkle Twinkle Little Star — 131 points on Hacker News

#9510. .dev vs .io vs .app vs .com - Choosing a Domain for Your Side Project (with Prices in India)

You've built the thing. It runs on localhost:3000, maybe on a free *.vercel.app or *.netlify.app subdomain. Now you want a real domain, and you're stuck between .dev, .io, .app and good old .com.

I run a small domain registration service in India, so I see this question a lot. Here's how I'd think about it, including the part most comparison posts skip: what you'll pay at renewal, not just in year one.

If you only read one line: pick .com if you can get a name you like, .dev or .app if the project is clearly a tool or an app, and .io only if the name is perfect and you're fine paying for it every year.

These are the prices on Namelume's pricing page at the time of writing (November 2026), in rupees:

Prices change, and every registrar prices differently, so check the live price before you buy anywhere.

The thing to notice is the renewal column. A lot of domains are sold cheap in year one and renew at a much higher price. For a side project that might sit quietly for three years before it takes off, the renewal price is the real price. Over three years:

That .io number is why I tell people to be sure before they pick it for a weekend project.

.com is what people type when they guess your URL. It's what autocomplete suggests. It's what your non-developer friends will assume.

Pick it when: the project could become a product people pay for, or you'll put the URL on anything printed, spoken or shared outside tech circles.

The catch: short, clean .com names are mostly gone. You'll often need two words (getthing.com, thinghq.com, usething.com). That's fine. A clear two-word .com usually beats a clever one-word name on an extension nobody remembers.

.dev is a generic extension (anyone can register it, anywhere) run by Google Registry. Its big technical feature is also its big gotcha: the whole .dev extension is on the HSTS preload list. Browsers will only ever load a .dev site over HTTPS.

Pick it when: it's a developer tool, a CLI's docs site, a component library, or your personal portfolio (yourname.dev is a popular pattern).

Skip it when: your audience isn't developers. To a shop owner or a customer, .dev means nothing.

.app is also run by Google Registry and also HSTS preloaded, so everything above about HTTPS applies here too.

Pick it when: the project is an app people use: a web app, a PWA, or the landing page for a mobile app. notesy.app tells people what it is before they click.

Watch out for: the renewal price is higher than the first-year price (₹2,179 first year, ₹2,739 renewal at the time of writing). Budget for the renewal, not the intro price.

.io became the startup and dev-tool favourite because "I/O" (input/output) reads nicely to programmers. But it's not a generic extension. It's the country code for the British Indian Ocean Territory.

Pick it when: you've found the perfect name, it's a dev tool or SaaS aimed at developers, and the yearly cost doesn't bother you.

There's no "best" extension, only the best fit for who will use your project and how long you'll keep it. Look at the renewal price, think about who needs to type the URL, and remember that .dev and .app won't load without HTTPS.

I'm building Namelume, a domain and hosting service for small businesses and makers in India. If you're stuck between two names for your project, drop them in the comments and I'll tell you which one I'd pick.

Starting a business in India? Namelume helps you find a name and register your domain, with clear prices in rupees.

#9509. Nigella Lawson’s Best Baking Advice Of All Time

There are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson. If she told me to put sardines in a birthday cake, I’d believe her. That’s just the kind of culinary authority you earn after nearly three decades of making us hungry through the TV screen. The cookbook author and television personality is now dishing out advice on The Great British Baking Show—she made her debut as a GBBS judge in September—but it’s just a small window into her extensive wisdom.

From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.

Cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does. “I think every recipe has to be as precise as possible,” Lawson told Vogue in 2018. “Baking, you have to be really precise. If you’re cooking and it suggests 2 to 3 carrots, it doesn’t really matter because they can be different sizes. It’s not going to alter the taste.”

So, you’ve never really baked before. It’s okay to start small! A three-tier chantilly cake your first day in the kitchen probably isn’t your best bet. “It’s important to go for a simple recipe. Read through the recipe to make sure you understand everything that’s being told to you at the time,” she said. “Look for a recipe that gives you an indication of what to do at each stage. This is what I always say to people: remind yourself you’re not running a restaurant.”

If you’ve been making your chocolate cake with milk, here’s your sign to stop. Lawson suggests swapping the dairy for hot or boiling water instead to “bloom” the cocoa, dissolve the sugar, and loosen the batter. The result? A crazy moist crumb!

Instead of using plain water when baking bread, Lawson suggests swapping it out for leftover pasta or potato water. “It will help the bread’s texture and rise,” she wrote on X in 2020. “Taste it before adding, though. If very salty, dilute it with fresh water and, obviously, leave any salt in the recipe out.”

It might sound weird, but Lawson swears by cream of tartar for fluffier, softer scones. “These are the best [ones] I’ve ever eaten, which is quite how it should be since they emanate from one of those old-fashioned cooks who starts a batch the minute the doorbell rings at teatime,” she wrote on her website in 2017. “Yes, I know they look as if they’ve got cellulite—it’s the cream of tartar, which is also why, despite their apparent solidity, they have that dreamy lightness.”

Lawson’s genius baking hack? DIY self-rising flour. “Nigella tends not to use self-raising flour in her more recent books as she doesn’t bother to keep both plain (all-purpose) and self-raising flour,” her site reads. “Partly because keeping just one type of flour saves on storage space, and partly because if you don’t use self-raising flour regularly, then it will lose its raising power over time.”

Instead, simply add 2 teaspoons of baking powder for each cup of plain flour. Sift the flour and baking powder together into a bowl before using (and make sure the baking powder is fully integrated), and you’re golden!

We’re all a little extra busy around the holidays, so if you’re planning a dinner party or holiday get-together, it’s okay to make shortcuts. Even Lawson says not everything has to be baked from scratch.

“I have a bit of a weakness for this sort of cake, which is essentially an assembly-job number, a construction of alternate layers of a rich, boozy cream and some store-bought sponge or other,” she told the BBC in 2023 about one of her favorite holiday desserts. “Here the layers comprise a confection of cream and mascarpone, seasonally spiked with Advocaat, full of crystallized ginger, figs and nuts, and that essential component of Christmas: gingerbread.”

Even Lawson admits: “just the words ‘uniformity of size and shape’ make [her] quake.” Hello, crazy foreshadowing for her future on GBBS.

“I am not in the slightest bit insecure about what I can bake, and I’m so very happy doing it, but shop-bought perfection is way beyond me,” she said in a 2014 interview with The Guardian. “But I’m perfectly content with that, and with the ramshackle homemade-ness of my creations.” If that’s good enough for Nigella, it’s good enough for me!

#9507. Migrating from mypy & pyright to Astral's ty in One Command

Python tooling has consolidated fast around Astral's stack: uv for packages, ruff for linting and formatting, and ty for Rust-speed static type checking.

While migrate-to-uv handles moving away from Poetry/Pipenv, moving an existing codebase from mypy, pyright, or basedpyright to ty still had a tedious manual step:

So I built ty-migrate — a zero-dependency Python 3.11+ CLI published on PyPI.

Preview what would change on your project without modifying any files:

Apply the migration and immediately verify with ty check:

Instead of naive key renaming, it maps settings into ty's actual structure:

Regex find-and-replace over Python source files inevitably corrupts docstrings, test fixtures, or string literals mentioning # type: ignore.

ty-migrate uses Python's standard-library tokenize module so only real COMMENT tokens are rewritten:

By default, bare # type: ignore and unmapped plugin error codes are left untouched (--unmapped-strategy keep) rather than silently widening ignores.

ty has real behavioral differences from mypy and pyright — for instance, ty checks unannotated function bodies unconditionally (check_untyped_defs is always on), has no single strict = True flag, and does not run mypy plugins.

Rather than silently ignoring those keys, --report breaks every option down into Translated, Guidance / Implicit in ty, and Unmapped, and --check returns exit code 3 in CI if anything needs manual review.

If you try it on a real codebase and hit an unmapped error code or edge case, open an issue or PR!

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

Sounds like you're biased for Grammarly. Not really that informative if you're already leaning towards one to begin with. Still, it was an interesting read. Tell me, do you use Grammarly with your day-to-day writing/blogging?

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

The logic is deliberately protective-first: a method that fails on compliance can mean confiscated goods at security — a total loss — and one that fails on protection produces dead-on-arrival electronics. Cost and convenience only break ties among methods that pass both gates.

Airlines and regulators differ on watt-hour limits and quantity caps, so confirm with your carrier. The practical rule is simple: batteries in the cabin, devices with installed batteries can usually be checked but are safer carried on. This is the single most common cause of confiscation at security, and it is entirely avoidable.

It depends on your destination country's personal exemption threshold and on whether the goods read as personal versus commercial — check your home country's rules before you fly, since thresholds vary widely. Packing electronics for the flight home is really a compliance problem wrapped in a protection problem: get the battery rules and the impact protection right, and the rest is optimization.

Choose TOP1 (modular hard-shell carry-on with inventory list) if you spent real money, bought anything fragile, or want a system you can reuse on the next sourcing trip. Choose TOP3 through TOP5 as complements or specialists: retail packaging for boxed goods, compression pouches to reclaim space, and courier shipping when volume or battery content makes flying impractical.

The common thread across every tier is the same: keep batteries in the cabin, keep a written record of what you bought, and match the protection level to the value of what is inside the bag. Do those three things, and the packing method becomes a detail rather than a risk.

#9501. A 167-Year-Old Mathematical Mystery, Two Claimed Proofs, and the Role of AI

Crypto Trader 💹 | REALTOR | Bitcoin Capitalist 🪙 | Building Africa's Super AI Robotics Company | Gugu Robotics

The biggest lie of the AI era? Believing that anyone who knows how to hit enter will become an author, a designer, or a thinker.

Crypto Trader 💹 | REALTOR | Bitcoin Capitalist 🪙 | Building Africa's Super AI Robotics Company | Gugu Robotics

The biggest lie of the AI era? Believing that anyone who knows how to hit enter will become an author, a designer, or a thinker.

Crypto Trader 💹 | REALTOR | Bitcoin Capitalist 🪙 | Building Africa's Super AI Robotics Company | Gugu Robotics

The biggest lie of the AI era? Believing that anyone who knows how to hit enter will become an author, a designer, or a thinker.

It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.

The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.

Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this …

For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.

But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯.

It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified.

Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully.

Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.

Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.

Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.

Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Society, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”

Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it.

In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”

#9499. 9 IDEs com IA para Linux em 2026: comparação de instalação, custos e modelos

Posted on Nov 25 • Originally published at guiadeti.com.br

Nove IDEs com IA para Linux diferem no modo de instalação, na cobrança, nos requisitos de conta e no suporte a modelos locais. Cursor, Devin Desktop, Kiro, Google Antigravity, Zed, Trae, VS Code com GitHub Copilot, IDEs JetBrains e Claude Code atendem a necessidades distintas; a escolha depende também da distribuição e do hardware disponíveis.

Cursor oferece pacotes .deb e RPM, além de AppImage. A empresa recomenda os repositórios APT e YUM para atualizar o editor junto com o sistema; o APT atende às arquiteturas amd64 e arm64. Em instalações novas de Ubuntu ou Debian, este primeiro comando instala os utilitários necessários para configurar o repositório:

sudo apt install -y curl gnupg curl -fsSL https://downloads.cursor.com/keys/anysphere.asc | gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/cursor.gpg >/dev/null echo "deb [arch=amd64,arm64 signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/cursor.gpg] https://downloads.cursor.com/aptrepo stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/cursor.list >/dev/null sudo apt update && sudo apt install cursor

O Devin Desktop, antigo Windsurf, manteve os repositórios APT e DNF após a mudança de nome. As URLs ainda usam o nome Windsurf, mas o pacote antigo encaminha a instalação para devin-desktop. O tarball não se atualiza sozinho; para instalar pelo APT, os comandos publicados são:

wget -qO- "https://windsurf-stable.codeiumdata.com/wVxQEIWkwPUEAGf3/windsurf.gpg" | gpg --dearmor > windsurf-stable.gpg sudo install -D -o root -g root -m 644 windsurf-stable.gpg /etc/apt/keyrings/windsurf-stable.gpg echo "deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/windsurf-stable.gpg] https://windsurf-stable.codeiumdata.com/wVxQEIWkwPUEAGf3/apt stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/windsurf.list >/dev/null sudo apt update && sudo apt install devin-desktop

Kiro lista suporte a Ubuntu 24 ou posterior, Debian 13 ou posterior, Fedora 40 ou posterior, Arch e Mint 22 ou posterior, em x86_64 e ARM64. O acesso exige autenticação por Google, GitHub, AWS Builder ID ou identidade organizacional; versões antigas também têm prazos de desativação que exigem atenção.

O Google Antigravity distribui a IDE para Linux como arquivo .tar.gz para x64 e ARM64, sem repositório nem pacotes .deb ou RPM. Assim, a instalação, a criação de uma entrada na área de trabalho e as atualizações ficam a cargo do usuário, um ponto importante em máquinas administradas por gerenciadores de pacotes.

Zed é um editor nativo em Rust que integra modelos locais por Ollama, LM Studio e llama.cpp. O plano Personal aceita chaves próprias de API e agentes externos, mas a versão oficial é distribuída por um script e exige GPU compatível com Vulkan. O comando de instalação do projeto é:

O Zed configura por padrão uma janela de contexto de 4.096 tokens para Ollama, valor pequeno para trabalho com agentes; é possível aumentá-la nas configurações do provedor. A IDE também integra agentes como Claude, Codex, OpenCode, Copilot e Cursor pelo Agent Client Protocol, cada um faturado pela própria conta.

VS Code com GitHub Copilot oferece repositórios APT e DNF, além de pacotes .deb, RPM e snap. O editor aceita chaves próprias no recurso Language Models e modelos locais pela extensão Ollama, permitindo usar o ambiente sem depender dos modelos hospedados pelo Copilot.

As IDEs JetBrains são voltadas a quem depende de recursos de refatoração em projetos Java, Kotlin ou Python. A instalação no Linux é feita pelo tarball do Toolbox App, e a ativação das licenças exige uma conta JetBrains. O AI Assistant aceita Ollama, LM Studio e chaves próprias de Anthropic, OpenAI ou Google, mas modelos locais ficam restritos a chat e conclusão de código, não aos agentes.

Claude Code separa o editor do agente: pode ser usado no terminal integrado do VS Code ou no painel do Zed, enquanto a cobrança fica vinculada à conta Claude. A instalação nativa usa o comando abaixo; o caminho local com Ollama exige modelo configurado para uma janela de contexto de pelo menos 64 mil tokens:

curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash ollama launch claude

Cursor tem opção gratuita e planos mensais de US$ 8 no Plus, US$ 30 no Premium, US$ 100 no Super e US$ 200 no Ultra. O Plus se limita aos modelos Grok e Composer; modelos de terceiros começam no Premium e podem acrescentar cobrança pelo preço de API, paga com créditos pré-pagos.

Devin Desktop oferece plano gratuito com cota limitada e conclusões Tab ilimitadas, Pro por US$ 20, Max por US$ 200 e Teams por US$ 80 mensais mais US$ 40 por assento. O uso acima da cota é cobrado por preço de API, sem uma tarifa por crédito informada para estimar meses de uso intenso.

Kiro disponibiliza 50 créditos no plano gratuito; o Pro custa US$ 20 por 1.000 créditos, Pro+ custa US$ 40 por 2.000, Pro Max custa US$ 100 por 5.000 e Power custa US$ 200 por 10.000. Créditos adicionais custam US$ 0,04 cada, o que permite calcular previamente o gasto conforme o consumo.

Google Antigravity tem um plano individual gratuito com limites semanais e conclusões Tab ilimitadas. Google AI Pro e Ultra aumentam os limites e incluem créditos de IA; modelos de terceiros ficam restritos ao Ultra, não há suporte a chave própria e a oferta empresarial ligada ao Gemini Enterprise começa em US$ 30 por assento.

No GitHub Copilot, o plano gratuito inclui 2.000 conclusões por mês e chat limitado. Pro custa US$ 10 com 1.500 créditos de IA, Pro+ custa US$ 39 com 7.000 e Max custa US$ 100 com 20.000; os planos pagos oferecem conclusões ilimitadas e créditos extras a US$ 0,01 cada.

Trae oferece 5.000 conclusões mensais no plano gratuito. O Pro custa US$ 20 e inclui US$ 20 em uso de modelos; Pro+ custa US$ 60 e Ultra, US$ 200. O uso exige uma conta, e a empresa recomenda consultar os termos de privacidade antes de conectar repositórios privados.

O JetBrains AI Free inclui 3 créditos a cada 30 dias. Para pessoas físicas, AI Pro custa US$ 10 e AI Ultimate, US$ 30 por 30 dias, antes de impostos e com cobrança na moeda local; cada crédito equivale a US$ 1 em uso de IA.

Zed Pro inclui US$ 5 em créditos de uso, e depois cobra pelos modelos hospedados conforme o preço de lista da API mais 10%. Claude Pro custa US$ 20 por mês ou US$ 17 mensais no pagamento anual; Claude Code não está incluído no plano gratuito.

Para instalações gerenciadas por repositórios, Devin Desktop, Cursor e VS Code têm caminhos integrados aos gerenciadores de pacotes. Antigravity depende de tarball, enquanto Zed usa seu instalador oficial e não oferece pacote oficial .deb ou RPM, embora existam opções mantidas pela comunidade.

Para executar modelos no próprio computador, Zed e VS Code com Ollama são alternativas; Kiro não oferece suporte a modelos locais. Zed exige aceleração Vulkan e pode não ser adequado a máquinas virtuais ou sessões remotas sem GPU, enquanto o uso do agente local do Ollama requer atenção à janela de contexto.

A decisão também passa por autenticação, privacidade e previsibilidade de gastos: Devin exige uma conta Devin ou chave de API, e Trae exige conta e recomenda revisar seus termos. Planos com excedentes calculados pelo uso de API podem variar; Kiro, por sua vez, apresenta preços por crédito para facilitar a estimativa.

#9498. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9497. You May Be Thawing Your Turkey Wrong—Here’s How To Avoid Spreading Salmonella

A frozen bird can save you money, but cutting corners could come at a cost.

Thanksgiving is a marathon, not a sprint. And the most involved, time-consuming dish is undoubtedly the turkey. The centerpiece of your holiday table needs hours in the oven and at least a day of brining, but don't forget the time it takes to defrost beforehand, too.

Frozen turkeys are generally the more accessible and affordable option. But they do require a little extra TLC and planning. So if you buy a frozen bird this year, you'll need to know how to work with it.

Making sure it tastes good is one thing, but ensuring that it's safe to eat is something else entirely. Like chicken, turkey can spread Salmonella and other harmful bacteria. You should exercise caution at every stage of the process, including thawing, to avoid making your guests sick. Here’s what you should know.

The USDA says it's also safe to defrost turkey in cold water, but in our opinion, it's not worth the hassle. The best bet is to thaw it in the refrigerator, where the bird can gradually defrost at the safe temperature with less risk of bacterial growth. What you should never do: thaw it on the counter, in the garage, or with warm water.

These environments are less controlled and can expose the turkey to the temperature danger zone (between 40°F and 140°F), where germs grow rapidly. Even if the center of the turkey is still frozen, the thawed exterior can become a hotbed for Salmonella by the time you're ready to roast.

Roasted turkey drippings make great gravy. But raw turkey juice dripping all over your fridge? Not so much. Even shrink-wrapped birds can leak, so you should always store your turkey on a baking sheet or roasting pan while it thaws.

Food safety experts also recommend storing raw meat on the lowest shelf. That way, any leaks are less likely to drip onto other ingredients in your fridge.

We know you're probably keeping a lot of other ingredients in your fridge, so it can be hard to set aside extra room for the turkey. That said, it's a step worth doing. Giving your turkey plenty of personal space minimizes the risk of raw meat or its juices coming into contact with other ingredients.

In the event that your turkey does contaminate another ingredient, here's what to know: Foods that won’t be cooked, like salad greens, should be tossed if they’ve come into contact with raw turkey juices. Cooking contaminated foods thoroughly can kill harmful bacteria, but you’ll also need to clean any surfaces the juices touched.

Turkeys are big, so they take a long time to thaw all the way through. The experts at Butterball say you should allocate a day for every four pounds of turkey if you're keeping it in the fridge. That means if you're working with a 16-pound bird, set aside four days just for defrosting. Once it's fully thawed, Butterball says your turkey will stay safe in the fridge for up to four days.

And on top of that, brining can make your turkey even more flavorful. If your frozen bird didn’t come pre-seasoned, consider setting aside another day or two for that step. (Want some guidance? Check out our brining guide.)

It’s extremely important to keep things clean while you’re handling a turkey. One of the most common ways Salmonella spreads in the kitchen is through cross-contamination caused by poor hygiene.

So wash those hands (including under your fingernails!) with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Make sure you also thoroughly clean any utensils and surfaces that come into contact with raw turkey or its juices using hot, soapy water.

And above all, don’t stress! Americans prepare millions of turkeys every Thanksgiving, so you're not alone in your turkey-roasting journey. Follow the tips above to ensure yours turns out safe to eat and delicious.

#9496. The AI Investment Race Has More Than One Winning Strategy

Engineer, strategist, product manager. Passionate about product and its business, financial, and societal implications.

Engineer, strategist, product manager. Passionate about product and its business, financial, and societal implications.

Engineer, strategist, product manager. Passionate about product and its business, financial, and societal implications.

By the end of October 2026, Apple's shares had gained approximately 27% for the year. [1] Its performance raises a strategic question for anyone deciding how much their company should invest in artificial intelligence: how much of the technology do you actually need to own to benefit from it?

The company's financial statements reveal a less obvious pattern. In fiscal 2026, the company spent $9.0 billion on property, plant and equipment, down from $12.7 billion a year earlier. Its research and development expense moved in the other direction, rising from $34.6 billion to $45.8 billion. Apple identified infrastructure costs, including AI investments, and employee costs as contributors to the R&D increase. [2] [3]

These are company-wide accounting measures. Neither tells us Apple's total AI spending, and the stock's performance does not establish that a particular AI strategy caused the return. But the combination challenges the usefulness of treating capital expenditure as a scoreboard for AI ambition.

Apple is also choosing where to rely on another company's capabilities. In January 2026, Apple and Google announced a multiyear collaboration under which Google's Gemini models and cloud technology would underpin the next generation of Apple Foundation Models. Their statement said Apple Intelligence would continue to operate on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute. [4]

A company can invest substantially in delivering AI to customers while making selective choices about which parts of the technology to develop itself. Whether that approach succeeds depends on how its industry evolves and where it can retain economic value.

I find it more useful to begin an AI investment discussion with strategic scenarios. A company can assess how its position would change if capable models became inexpensive and interchangeable, or if an AI assistant became the customer's main route to a purchase. Those futures put different assets at risk and create different opportunities.

Each possibility creates a different reason to invest. Several can apply to the same company at the same time. The resulting investment portfolio may include proprietary development, commercial software, partnerships, and experiments whose purpose is to resolve an important uncertainty.

Buy or partner; invest in product and workflow integration

Supplier alternatives, switching cost, customer value

Develop the capabilities that support a lasting advantage

Willingness to pay, performance, replicability

Defend or redesign how customers reach the business

Where journeys start, retention, monetization

Deploy proven solutions against operating outcomes

Cost per outcome, service quality, rework

Consider the first scenario: capable AI becomes widely available, while the company's existing products and customer relationships remain commercially valuable.

There is evidence that some AI capabilities have become dramatically cheaper to access. Stanford's 2025 AI Index reported that the inference cost of reaching GPT-3.5-level performance declined by more than a factor of 280 between November 2022 and October 2024. This describes a benchmark-specific historical change, rather than a forecast for total enterprise AI costs. [5]

Nevertheless, it illustrates a commercially attractive possibility for a company with valuable distribution. Competing technology suppliers could improve the capabilities available to that company while reducing the price of obtaining them. The company can then concentrate investment on the customer experience and the systems through which those capabilities are delivered.

This is one way to interpret Apple's partnership approach. If customers continue to value its devices and ecosystem, Apple could benefit as external models improve. Owning the customer experience could prove more valuable than independently recreating every underlying capability. That is a strategic hypothesis, not a conclusion that the partnership has already established.

The investment implication extends beyond consumer technology. A regional distributor could buy a capable language model while developing the integrations that connect customer requests to its inventory, pricing, and delivery systems. The distributor would still need to invest in reliable execution. It would have little reason to train a general-purpose model unless owning that capability created a demonstrable advantage.

This scenario favors buying or partnering for widely available capabilities and retaining control over the parts of the service that customers value. The company should also preserve its ability to switch suppliers. A low initial price is less attractive if changing providers later requires rebuilding the business.

The second scenario is that AI creates product differentiation customers will pay for, and the company possesses assets that make that differentiation difficult to reproduce.

John Deere's See & Spray provides a concrete example of the kind of capability involved. The system combines computer vision with machinery to identify plants and target spraying. Blue River Technology reports that the technology was used across more than five million acres in 2025 and that customers reduced non-residual herbicide use by nearly 50%. These are supplier-reported results, and reduced herbicide use is not the same as a 50% reduction in total farming costs. [6]

The strategic opportunity is the combination of perception, physical equipment, and dependable performance in the field. For an equipment manufacturer, investing in that combination can support a differentiated product. An agricultural customer buys an operating result: effective weed control at an attractive total cost.

Those are different investment cases for the same technology. Deere must assess whether its product development generates customer demand and returns it can sustain against competitors. A farmer must assess whether the savings and other benefits justify the equipment, licensing, maintenance, and operating costs under local conditions.

This distinction also limits the argument for building proprietary AI. Access to internal data is a starting point. The company must show that the data improves an outcome customers value, that competitors cannot readily reproduce the result, and that maintaining the capability is economically attractive. Custom development without those conditions can leave the company maintaining expensive technology with little commercial distinction.

Investments in this scenario deserve measures of differentiation: willingness to pay, customer retention, product adoption, or a sustained performance advantage. A product team that demonstrates a better model benchmark still needs to establish that the improvement matters to a buyer.

The third scenario is that AI changes how customers find, select, or purchase products, putting an existing source of revenue at risk.

Google Search illustrates the scale of the strategic exposure. Google Search & other generated $63.35 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up from $56.57 billion a year earlier. Those figures are revenue attributable to existing business, not necessarily one created by AI. [7]

If more customers begin their research or purchasing journeys inside AI assistants, the business that controls those interactions could gain influence over which suppliers are considered and how transactions are completed. For an incumbent, investing in the new interface can therefore have a defensive purpose even when its immediate monetization is uncertain.

The relevant comparison includes the outcome of allowing another company to take that position. A proposal can look unattractive against today's business and attractive against a credible scenario in which customer access deteriorates. That comparison requires evidence about customer behavior and plausible estimates of revenue at risk.

Calling an investment defensive should not give it an unlimited budget. Management should specify which customer behavior it is trying to protect, how quickly that behavior could change, and whether a partnership could achieve the same objective with less capital. Milestones might include retaining valuable customer journeys, matching an emerging service expectation, or establishing a viable way to monetize a new interaction.

Apple can face this scenario alongside the first. Affordable external models could strengthen its products, while independent AI assistants could also change how customers use devices and applications. Partnering for model capability and investing to retain influence over the customer experience can therefore be consistent parts of the same strategy.

The fourth scenario is that AI improves operating performance while the main reasons customers choose the company remain broadly intact.

A study published in The Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2025 examined an AI assistant used by 5,172 customer-support agents. Access to the assistant increased issues resolved per hour by 15% on average. Less experienced and lower-skilled workers saw gains of approximately 30%, while results differed substantially for more experienced workers. These findings came from one company and should not be treated as a universal forecast. [8]

For a business buying such a capability, the investment case can be attractive without requiring ownership of a foundation model. The work is to select a suitable system, connect it to reliable information, and redesign the service process so improved performance translates into a useful result.

The uneven gains in the study also matter for capital allocation. A company may obtain better returns by concentrating implementation and training on the employees or workflows that benefit most. Distributing identical tools to everyone is a deployment choice; it does not establish the best allocation of spending.

In this scenario, operating measures should carry most of the burden of proof. A customer-service investment might be judged on the cost of a successfully resolved issue, repeat contacts, and customer satisfaction. These measures help prevent apparent speed improvements from being purchased through poorer service or additional work elsewhere.

The farmer buying See & Spray also fits this scenario. The technology may be strategically differentiating for its developer while functioning as an efficiency investment for its customer. Its classification depends on whose business case is being evaluated.

The framework becomes more useful when we apply several scenarios to one company. Alphabet provides a particularly clear example because it develops AI, sells AI-related services, and uses AI internally.

Search gives Alphabet an existing business to defend as customer behavior changes. Google Cloud creates an opportunity to sell capabilities to other companies: its third-quarter 2026 revenue was $30.71 billion, with operating income of $11.12 billion. Those are segment results across Cloud's business, not a measurement of standalone AI returns. [7]

Alphabet also uses the technology to improve its own operations. On its October 2026 earnings call, management said selected teams across Chrome, Ads, and Search had recently used a new model to ship 35% more code with 30% fewer errors. This is a company-reported claim about selected teams over a short period, rather than an independently established company-wide productivity result. [9]

The same company develops AI, sells capabilities to customers and uses the technology internally

Retain valuable customer journeys and sustain monetization

$30.71B revenue Q3 2026, total Cloud Segment

Earn returns on infrastructure and services sold to customers

Improve useful output and reliability at an attractive cost

*Management reported for selected Chrome, Ads & Search teams over recent weeks

Exhibit 4. Search, Cloud, and internal engineering illustrate different strategic investment motives within Alphabet. Financial data: Q3 2026 results [7]. Engineering claims: October 2026 earnings call [9]. Strategic classification: Author analysis. Business revenue is not AI-attributed revenue; engineering metrics cover selected teams and are company-reported.

The three uses call for different investment tests. Search requires an assessment of customer access and monetization. Cloud requires an assessment of demand, utilization, and returns on the infrastructure needed to serve customers. Internal engineering tools require evidence about accepted output, reliability, and the time required to deliver useful changes.

They may share models and infrastructure. That can make a common investment more attractive, but it also creates an accounting challenge. Shared costs must be recognized, and benefits must not be counted repeatedly in separate business cases. Revenue from selling a capability and savings from using it internally need distinct, defensible estimates.

A single corporate label such as 'aggressive AI investor' conceals these differences. A company can rationally build a specialized capability for one business, partner for another, and buy conventional software for a third. The relevant unit of analysis is the business activity and the value it creates or protects.

Scenario planning should then influence the timing of investment. A company does not need certainty about the eventual market structure before taking action. It needs to understand which commitments are difficult to reverse and which actions improve its ability to respond as evidence develops.

Reliable data, integration skills, and the ability to evaluate AI on actual business tasks can be useful across several futures. Large infrastructure commitments or dependence on a single supplier may be harder to reverse. The sequence should reflect both the value of learning and the cost of delay. Where experience compounds or customer relationships are being established quickly, waiting can itself be expensive.

One practical approach is to ask each investment sponsor to document the scenario supporting the proposal, the capability the company must control, and the evidence that would change the decision. The initial funding can then match what is currently known, with additional commitments tied to specific findings.

For a distributor buying external models, the review could track whether suppliers remain interchangeable on actual customer tasks and whether switching costs are rising. For an equipment manufacturer, it could examine whether a specialized AI feature produces customer benefits that competing systems cannot match economically. For a business exposed to new AI intermediaries, it could track changes in where valuable customer journeys begin.

These signals should have consequences. A persistent performance advantage might support more proprietary development. Improving vendor alternatives could justify shifting resources toward integration and customer service. A sustained movement of customers to a new interface could accelerate a defensive investment. A project that repeatedly misses its operating objectives should face a funding decision even if the underlying technology continues to improve.

This also changes how an executive team should discuss the total AI budget. A company should be able to explain how much is supporting proven operating improvements, how much is developing a distinctive offering, and how much is protecting customer access or resolving uncertainty. The balance will change as evidence accumulates. There is no reason to expect the right allocation to be identical across businesses.

Apple's approach is interesting because it brings those choices into view. Its long-term success will depend on the capabilities it builds, the relationships it retains, and the terms on which it can obtain technology from others. The size of a capital-spending announcement captures only part of that decision.

An AI investment strategy should explain the future the company is preparing for, the value it expects to capture in that future, and the capabilities it must control to do so. It should also identify the evidence that would lead management to invest more, change partners, or stop. That gives leaders a basis for deciding how much to spend and where each additional dollar belongs.

[1] The Washington Post, November 3, 2026Apple share-price gain through October 2026 only. No causal inference.

[2] Apple FY2026 consolidated financial statements, November 2, 2026FY2025 and FY2026 cash payments for PP&E and total R&D expense.

[3] Apple FY2026 Form 10-K, Operating ExpensesExplanation of R&D growth; company-wide measures do not isolate AI.

[4] Joint statement from Google and Apple, January 12, 2026Multiyear collaboration, Gemini and cloud technology, devices and Private Cloud Compute.

[5] Stanford HAI, 2025 AI Index Report, takeaway 7More than 280-fold inference cost decline at GPT-3.5-level performance from November 2022 to October 2024.

[6] Blue River Technology, Products, See & Spray 2025 resultsComputer vision and machinery; more than five million acres and nearly 50% reduction in non-residual herbicide use. Supplier-reported results.

[7] Alphabet third-quarter 2026 results, October 28, 2026Google Search & other and Cloud revenue; Cloud operating income. These are total business/segment measures, not AI-attributed results.

[8] Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, Generative AI at Work, Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2), 2025, pp. 889-942Published version: 5,172 agents, 15% average gain, approximately 30% for less experienced and lower-skilled workers; single-firm study.

[9] Alphabet third-quarter 2026 earnings call, October 28, 2026Management's recent selected-team engineering claims: 35% more code shipped and 30% fewer errors. Not an independently established company-wide effect.

#9494. We ran our despatch scheduler as a StatefulSet so it could never run twice, and that kept it stopped for two hours

Our despatch scheduler batches orders into carrier collections, and it must never run as two copies at once, or the same orders go into two collections. So it runs in Kubernetes as a StatefulSet with one replica. A Deployment's rolling update starts a new pod before the old one has gone. A StatefulSet promises at most one pod with a given name, which was exactly the guarantee we wanted.

On a Tuesday in October, at ten past two, the virtual machine under that pod hung. The kernel stopped responding, but the hypervisor still reported the machine as running, so it stayed in the cluster. Within a minute the node was NotReady. Five minutes later Kubernetes marked the scheduler's pod for deletion, as it does by default for pods on an unreachable node. Then nothing happened for the next hour and fifty minutes. Two afternoon collections left without the orders meant for them.

A pod on an unreachable node cannot be confirmed dead, because the only thing that could confirm it is the kubelet on that node. So the pod sat in Terminating. A ReplicaSet would have started a replacement elsewhere straight away, since it does not count terminating pods. A StatefulSet will not create despatch-scheduler-0 again until the old despatch-scheduler-0 is gone from the API server, because the old one might still be running on a machine nobody can see. The guarantee we chose the StatefulSet for was working perfectly. It had no way to tell a hung machine from a busy one.

At four o'clock an engineer found the pod in Terminating, deleted it with --force, and the scheduler started on another node within a minute.

Force deletion is only safe if the old copy really is stopped, so our runbook now begins with fencing: power the virtual machine off through the cloud API and confirm it is off. Then we apply the node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service taint, stable since Kubernetes 1.28, which deletes the pods on that node and detaches its volumes without waiting for a kubelet that is never coming back. We have alerts on any pod in Terminating for more than ten minutes, and on any StatefulSet with fewer ready replicas than desired.

At most one, done safely, sometimes means none, and somebody has to be told when it does.
