#9492. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9489. How to Generate a Random String (Secure & Easy Methods in JavaScript, Python, PHP & Bash)

Learn how to generate a random string in JavaScript, Python, PHP, and Bash. Avoid the Math.random() trap and copy secure examples for tokens and IDs.

A random string shows up everywhere: session IDs, API keys, password reset tokens, temporary file names, and unique database identifiers. Most of us write a quick helper for it, and it works fine until someone asks whether the string is predictable.

That question matters more than it sounds. In JavaScript, Math.random() looks random, but it is a pseudo-random generator. If an attacker can observe enough of its output, they can predict the next values. Using it for a password reset token or an API key creates a real security hole.

The fix is a cryptographically secure random number generator (CSPRNG) plus a charset and length that fit the use case.

Browser-safe version with crypto.getRandomValues():

The % in the browser example introduces a small modulo bias, because 256 isn't evenly divisible by 62. For most apps that's acceptable. For strict requirements, use rejection sampling or the hex/base64 output from randomBytes().

Don't do this for anything security-related:

Use the secrets module (Python 3.6+). The random module is not suitable for tokens.

rand() and mt_rand() are not cryptographically secure. Use random_int() and random_bytes() (PHP 7+).

As a rule of thumb, security tokens should carry at least 128 bits of randomness. Sixteen random bytes gives you that.

What's the best way to generate a random string? Use a CSPRNG: secrets in Python, crypto.randomBytes() or crypto.getRandomValues() in JavaScript, and random_bytes() or random_int() in PHP.

Is Math.random() safe for passwords or tokens? No. It isn't cryptographically secure, and its output can be predicted.

How long should a random string be? For security tokens, aim for at least 128 bits, about 22 alphanumeric characters or 16 random bytes in hex.

Can two random strings ever be the same? Yes, though it's extremely unlikely with long strings. Enforce uniqueness at the database level if the value must be unique.

#9487. Your Lead Score May Be Learning Who Sales Already Chose to Call

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Hero illustration. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

Consider a hypothetical company that trains a lead score on historical customers. The model discovers that contacts from a favored segment are more likely to progress. Sales receives more contacts from that segment, calls them sooner, and creates more opportunities there.

The next training cycle sees the same pattern more strongly.

That pattern could reflect real demand. It could also reflect where the company invested its attention. Historical success does not explain the difference by itself.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.

I would not reject lead scoring because of this problem. I would ask a more precise question before allowing a score to allocate scarce sales capacity: what process produced the labels that the system is learning to predict?

Consider the label sales-qualified lead. It may represent a carefully verified need. In another organization, it may represent a rep clicking a lifecycle field after a first call. A label with the same name can encode different decisions.

Even a clear commercial outcome sits downstream of company actions. Routing, response time, territory coverage, pricing, product availability, and follow-up quality can affect who reaches that outcome. A model trained on the history may learn useful correlations without separating those mechanisms.

HubSpot's AI score documentation describes generating criteria and points from account contact data using a selected lifecycle transition. That makes the chosen transition an important modeling decision, not an administrative detail.

The implication is my analytical interpretation, not a claim that HubSpot's model has a particular defect: if the business meaning of the transition is unstable, the score's target is unstable too. Review the process behind the field before debating whether the suggested points look sensible.

Imagine a fictional business with two lead groups. Both contain potential buyers. Group A receives a fast response and several useful conversations. Group B is routed to an understaffed queue, where many records receive no meaningful follow-up.

If Group A progresses more often, that observation alone does not establish how Group B would perform under the same treatment. Nor does it establish that moving every Group B record into the fast queue would produce the same result.

Start by auditing the exposure to company action: assigned owner, attempted contact, reached contact, response delay, and relevant follow-up where those facts are available and appropriate to use. Missing activity is not always proof that no activity occurred, so mark coverage limitations.

Distinguish a negative outcome from an unresolved one. A prospect who declined after a relevant conversation is not equivalent to a lead that nobody reached. A lead created yesterday should not be labeled a failure merely because its outcome window has not elapsed.

This review does not solve causal inference. It tells the team whether its training labels mix meaningfully different situations and where stronger evaluation may be needed.

The sales-attention feedback loop. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

The most flattering model can be the one that has accidentally seen the future. A property added during a sales conversation may predict the later opportunity extremely well, but it cannot help prioritize the call that produced the property.

The scikit-learn guide to data leakage explains the general problem: information unavailable at prediction time can create overly optimistic evaluation. The principle applies whether a team uses that library, a managed product, or a spreadsheet.

Define a scoring timestamp and reconstruct the feature values available then. Keep event time separate from ingestion time. A warehouse record loaded on Friday may describe an interaction that occurred on Tuesday, while a value overwritten on Thursday may hide what was visible on Wednesday.

For a custom evaluation, inspect high-performing features for timing. Deal creation, later lifecycle stages, post-call qualification fields, and completed onboarding steps may belong to the outcome process rather than the pre-call decision.

Do not assume every predictive feature is leakage. A confirmed budget recorded before the scoring time can be legitimate. The test is availability and permitted use at the actual decision point, not whether the feature seems unusually informative.

HubSpot's scoring overview distinguishes engagement, fit, and combined scores, with capabilities depending on subscription and record type. These scores can be useful for prioritization without representing a calibrated chance of winning.

A score of eighty should not be presented as an eighty-percent probability unless the system and evaluation support that interpretation. Ranking quality and probability calibration answer different questions.

The scikit-learn calibration documentation provides the statistical distinction. A model can rank cases usefully while its stated probabilities fail to match observed frequencies. Calibration itself requires appropriate held-out evaluation.

For a marketing team, the practical consequence is simple. Name the output according to what it is. Priority score is safer than probability of purchase when the number is a weighted set of criteria. An AI-generated explanation should not upgrade the score's meaning in its prose.

This also affects thresholds. A cutoff chosen because sales can review fifty records is a capacity decision. It should not be described as a natural boundary between buyers and nonbuyers.

A global accuracy number can hide a poor allocation decision. If sales works only a small top-ranked queue, inspect the quality and coverage of that queue. If the score triggers nurturing rather than a call, evaluate the relevance and consequences of that different action.

Keep a later evaluation period separate from training and tuning. For custom models, ensure preprocessing and feature selection respect the split. When records from the same company are strongly related, consider whether a random contact split allows account-level information to leak across the boundary.

Report uncertainty and sample sizes. Three wins in a tiny group do not establish that a model works equally well there. An absence of observed failures can reflect a lack of evaluated cases.

The evaluation should also account for lead maturity. Compare cohorts with sufficient time to reach the defined outcome rather than rewarding the oldest records for having had more opportunities to progress.

Before changing routing, calculate the proposed score alongside the current process without allowing it to drive consequential actions. Record what it would recommend and why. This is shadow evaluation, not a controlled estimate of incremental value.

Review disagreements. Which promising-looking leads rank low? Which high-ranked leads have only noisy email activity? Are important product segments missing from the training history? Does the explanation depend on a property that sales fills only after qualification?

Then decide whether a limited, appropriately designed comparison is justified. A randomized routing experiment may be useful in some settings, but it requires ethical treatment, operational capacity, adequate measurement, and a clear fallback. Do not casually withhold responses to explicit requests for help.

If experimentation is not feasible, document the narrower evidence available. An observational comparison can guide improvement without proving that the score caused more revenue.

Keep the current policy and model version attached to each decision. Otherwise, a later review may compare outcomes across several routing changes while attributing everything to one new score.

A small pre-release test can expose a timing error without requiring a new model. Select one historical contact and write down:

Repeat for a contacted lead, an uncontacted lead, and an unresolved recent lead. These are diagnostic cases, not a representative performance sample. If the reconstruction cannot distinguish those paths, resolve the data-history problem before trusting a larger evaluation. A polished explanation cannot restore a feature snapshot that was never retained.

For each score release, retain the target definition, eligible population, feature timing assumptions, outcome window, evaluation period, routing action, capacity threshold, and known exclusions. Include the date and person responsible for reviewing business meaning.

Describe what changed from the previous version. A revised lifecycle policy may require a new evaluation even if the scoring formula barely changed. A new product or territory can create a population shift that historical averages do not capture.

Also define a stop condition. An unexplained drop in data completeness, a sudden score distribution change, or a mismatch between actual routing and documented policy should trigger investigation. A score should not remain authoritative just because it continues to produce numbers.

Review qualitative failures alongside aggregate metrics. A salesperson discovering that a high score came from machine-generated interaction is useful evidence about a signal problem. It is not proof that the entire model is worthless, but it should not disappear because the headline metric remains attractive.

There is another practical safeguard: retain a review route for records outside the highest-ranked queue. Without it, the organization can stop learning about the people its model consistently overlooks. The route might be a bounded manual audit, an approved exploration policy, or a segment-specific review, depending on the business and its obligations.

Do not call that review proof that every low-ranked lead deserves equal effort. It is a way to notice systematic blind spots and collect better evidence before making stronger allocation claims.

The review should have a defined sample, owner, and outcome taxonomy. Otherwise, a few memorable missed opportunities can dominate the discussion as easily as a flattering aggregate score. Both quantitative results and individual examples need a clear account of how they were selected.

The future of AI-assisted prioritization is not merely a more elaborate formula. It is a process that can distinguish what buyers did, what the company did, and what remains unknown.

A useful score can reduce wasted review time and make a team's reasoning more consistent. Those benefits still need verification in the actual workflow. They are not guaranteed by the presence of AI or by a strong historical correlation.

The question to take into the next scoring review is not only which leads converted. Ask which leads received a real opportunity to convert, what was known when they were prioritized, and whether the next policy will repeat the same blind spots.

That question turns scoring from a self-confirming ranking into a decision system the business can challenge and improve.

#9486. Panera Is Giving Away Free Baguettes Just In Time For Thanksgiving

Thanksgiving is stressful enough without realizing you’ve forgotten something at the grocery store. Between the turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, and countless other sides, there’s a lot to keep track of. Thankfully, Panera is stepping in to make sure you can cross at least one thing off your shopping list.

The bakery-café chain is giving away free baguettes on Wednesday, November 25, just in time for Thanksgiving dinner. And considering how expensive holiday grocery shopping can get, I’ll happily take a little free bread.

The giveaway is pretty straightforward: Starting at 11 a.m., customers can visit select participating Panera locations and receive a free baguette with any in-café purchase. That means you can stop by for your usual soup, sandwich, or coffee and leave with an extra loaf of bread for your Thanksgiving table.

Of course, there is one important catch: You’ll need to make a purchase to qualify, so the baguette isn’t entirely free with no strings attached. Plus, each participating café will have only 60 free baguettes on hand, limited to one per person, so you’ll need to act fast if you want to get your hands on one. You can check whether your local Panera is participating on Panera's website or app, or by contacting your local café.

The giveaway is part of Panera’s effort to bring its bread-making tradition to Thanksgiving celebrations nationwide. And while the holiday might be better known for dinner rolls and biscuits, I certainly wouldn’t complain about adding a baguette to the spread.

Having an extra loaf of bread around on Thanksgiving is never a bad idea. Between soaking up leftover gravy, serving alongside dinner, and making sandwiches with whatever turkey survives the night, there are plenty of ways to put it to good use.

And with the giveaway happening the day before Thanksgiving, the timing couldn’t be more convenient for anyone finishing up their last-minute holiday preparations.

#9484. AWS dobra para 30 minutos o timeout do Lambda sob demanda

Posted on Nov 25 • Originally published at guiadeti.com.br

A AWS dobrou de 15 para 30 minutos o tempo máximo de execução das funções de evento sob demanda do Lambda. A mudança vale em todas as regiões comerciais, sem adesão prévia e com os preços padrão. O novo limite pode ser configurado por função e se aplica a invocações síncronas, assíncronas e a mapeamentos de fontes de eventos.

O teto de 15 minutos estava em vigor desde 2018. Para ampliar o prazo, administradores precisam alterar a configuração de cada função; valores acima de 1.800 segundos são rejeitados com erro de validação. A AWS cita como casos de uso agentes de IA que encadeiam chamadas a modelos e ferramentas, transcodificação de mídia, simulações de Monte Carlo e geração de relatórios.

aws lambda update-function-configuration \ --function-name my-demo-function \ --timeout 1800

A atualização não uniformiza os limites de todos os formatos do serviço. Web Functions continuam com o máximo de 15 minutos, enquanto Lambda MicroVMs podem executar por até oito horas. Nas Lambda Managed Instances, invocações síncronas chegam a 30 minutos, mas as assíncronas mantêm o limite de 90 minutos introduzido em setembro.

Antes de aumentar o timeout, equipes devem recalcular a concorrência necessária. A AWS apresenta a relação entre concorrência, requisições por segundo e duração média em segundos: à mesma taxa de requisições, uma execução de 30 minutos exige o dobro da concorrência de uma execução de 15 minutos. Um fluxo de uma requisição por segundo durante 30 minutos requer 1.800 execuções simultâneas.

Para processamento com SQS, o timeout de visibilidade da fila deve ser pelo menos seis vezes o prazo da função, chegando a três horas quando ela pode executar por 30 minutos. Em Kinesis e DynamoDB Streams, cada shard entrega um lote por vez; por isso, uma função mais lenta também retarda o processamento daquele shard.

Há ainda diferenças nos mapeamentos de outras fontes. Mapeamentos de Amazon MQ, DocumentDB e Kafka criados antes de 19 de novembro permanecem limitados a 14 minutos. O gateway NAT encerra conexões ociosas após 350 segundos, e a fase Init da função continua sujeita ao limite de dez segundos.

O profissional de AWS Wibo van der Sluis testou a regra de visibilidade com uma função configurada para 1.800 segundos. No teste, uma fila com visibilidade de 90 minutos e depois de 60 segundos foi aceita enquanto o mapeamento já existia; um novo mapeamento para a mesma fila foi recusado. A validação ocorreu na criação, não em alterações posteriores.

Van der Sluis também observou que, na criação, a checagem comparou a fila ao timeout da função, e não ao múltiplo de seis recomendado. Equipes devem tratar essa relação como uma configuração operacional a garantir, em vez de depender exclusivamente da validação do serviço.

Em funções assíncronas que expiram três vezes, o evento pode acumular até 90 minutos de execução antes de chegar a uma fila de mensagens não entregues. Para tarefas longas, vale manter os handlers idempotentes e planejar retentativas e tratamento de trabalho parcial, pois uma falha no meio da execução pode deixar efeitos incompletos.

Um timeout maior não resolve necessariamente código lento atrás de uma API, e execuções longas precisam ser avaliadas pelo custo por invocação, que acompanha a memória configurada e o tempo usado. Para fluxos com várias etapas, estado explícito e retentativas, Step Functions com Fargate ou ECS pode oferecer uma estrutura mais adequada.

A mudança amplia o espaço de uso do Lambda para tarefas que ultrapassavam o limite anterior, mas não elimina diferenças de preço, concorrência e comportamento entre serviços. A escolha deve considerar duração, volume de chamadas, integração com filas ou streams e o modo como a aplicação recupera trabalho após falhas.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/aws-lambda-amplia-limite-timeout-30-minutos/

#9480. From Student to Open Source Contributor: My Journey with Dapr

I am Orlando Ezequiel Salazar Cruz, a Computer Systems Engineering student at the Instituto Tecnológico Superior de Calkiní (ITESCAM) in Campeche, Mexico. Throughout my coursework and personal projects, I have spent most of my time building web interfaces with Angular and TypeScript, along with backend services using Python and FastAPI.

When you are studying software engineering, distributed systems can easily feel like something reserved for senior engineers running large cloud clusters. You read about service discovery, retries, event-driven messaging, and fault tolerance, and it is easy to assume you need complex infrastructure before you can even start building.

Discovering Dapr (Distributed Application Runtime) gave me a much clearer way to understand distributed applications. It also gave me a realistic entry point into open source software, showing me that your first contributions do not have to be massive runtime features to be useful to other developers.

Dapr is an open-source, portable, event-driven runtime designed to help developers build resilient distributed applications across cloud and edge environments. Instead of requiring your application code to import vendor-specific SDKs or manage infrastructure clients directly, Dapr runs alongside your application—commonly as a sidecar process—and exposes standard HTTP and gRPC APIs.

Dapr separates what your application wants to do (such as saving state or publishing an event) from how the underlying infrastructure performs that operation (such as Redis, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, or cloud-managed services). Your code talks to the local Dapr sidecar over HTTP or gRPC, and Dapr handles the interaction with the configured component.

Distributed systems introduce failure modes that do not exist in a single-process application. Network requests fail, downstream services restart or slow down, and partial outages happen regularly.

Dapr helps reduce several common problems in microservice and distributed architectures:

One of the easiest ways to learn Dapr is through its building blocks. Each building block solves a specific distributed systems task while keeping your application code focused on business logic.

Service Invocation lets one service call another reliably using a Dapr app ID instead of hardcoding hostnames, ports, or network locations. Dapr handles discovery and routing through the sidecar layer, making service-to-service communication simpler across environments.

State Management provides a consistent API for saving, retrieving, updating, and deleting key-value state without coupling your code to a specific database driver. It also supports features like optimistic concurrency control (ETags), where supported by the state store, so multiple service instances can update shared state safely.

Bindings let your application react to external events (input bindings) or trigger external systems (output bindings) through a uniform interface—such as cron schedules, queues, storage buckets, or messaging systems—without writing custom integration code for each external service.

Secrets Management gives applications a standard way to retrieve sensitive values—such as API keys, database passwords, or tokens—from a configured secret store instead of hardcoding secrets or writing custom secret-loading logic in every service.

Workflows allow you to orchestrate long-running, stateful, multi-step processes across services and activities. If a process spans several steps or encounters transient failures and restarts, Dapr Workflows tracks execution state so the workflow can resume reliably.

Reading documentation helps you understand the APIs, while structured courses help connect the pieces together. Through Dapr University, I completed courses covering Dapr 101, Workflows, and Agents.

Because I already had experience building backend APIs with Python and FastAPI and frontends with Angular and TypeScript, these courses helped me connect distributed systems theory with practical service design. Dapr 101 gave me a solid foundation in the sidecar model and core building blocks, while the Workflows and Agents courses showed how multi-step orchestration and modern agentic workflows manage state and coordinate tasks reliably.

Learning one building block at a time made distributed architecture feel manageable instead of overwhelming.

For a long time, contributing to a well-known open-source repository felt intimidating. Looking at open issues and architecture discussions, it is easy to think a student has nothing useful to offer. Working in the Dapr repositories showed me that clear examples and accurate documentation are essential parts of any developer tool.

My first merged contribution in the Dapr ecosystem was dapr/js-sdk#848 ("docs: clarify handling of missing state"), which resolved issue #477 and was merged into main on October 18, 2026.

In the JavaScript SDK's gRPC state management example, a key named "key-2" was deleted and then queried afterward, but the example needed to show more clearly how to handle the case where the state value no longer exists. I updated the example to check for empty results and explicitly report when the state is missing, and I expanded the README to document how missing state and other HTTP errors are handled.

During the review process, a maintainer helped me understand the Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) requirement. I learned how to add Signed-off-by lines using git rebase and update my remote branch cleanly before the pull request was merged.

Another contribution I worked on is dapr/docs#5283 ("fix: correct Encrypt and Decrypt API label"), related to issue #5086.

In Dapr's cryptography documentation, an architecture diagram contained a typo—"Encrypt and Decrypt AI" instead of "Encrypt and Decrypt API". I corrected that label to "Encrypt and Decrypt API" while preserving the original layout and structure of the diagram.

The pull request was approved on October 16, 2026, and a maintainer also carried the change over to the v1.19 branch while preserving my authorship. At the time of writing, PR #5283 is approved and still open awaiting final merge.

Neither of these pull requests modified Dapr's internal runtime engine, yet both fixed real points of confusion that developers encounter when reading documentation or following SDK examples.

To show how the State Management building block works in practice, here is an illustrative example using Python and FastAPI alongside the Dapr State Management HTTP API.

This snippet is included for educational purposes to demonstrate the API contract and error handling rather than a deployment I have run or benchmarked for this post.

According to the official Dapr State API specification:

Here is how a FastAPI service can interact with a local Dapr sidecar on port 3500, translate Dapr's 204 missing-key response into a 404 for API consumers, and handle httpx connection or timeout errors cleanly:

Before running this example, make sure you have Python, Docker, and the Dapr CLI installed. The standard local Dapr initialization uses Docker to provision development dependencies, including a Redis state store.

For installation instructions, refer to the official Dapr documentation.

Save the code above as main.py and start the application alongside a Dapr sidecar configured with a local statestore component:

You can then open the FastAPI interactive documentation in your browser:

Handling the 204 No Content response explicitly is a good example of why reading API specifications and SDK examples carefully matters: if your service assumes every non-error response contains JSON, querying a missing key will fail at runtime.

Participating in real code reviews taught me several practical lessons that you rarely get from classroom assignments alone:

Focused contributions have real value: Clarifying missing-state behavior in an example, improving a README, or fixing a label in an architecture diagram prevents confusion for the next developer using the project.

Documentation is part of the developer experience: Good software is much harder to use when edge cases are undocumented or diagrams contain typos.

Git workflow and DCO discipline matter: Keeping clean commits, rebasing when asked, and including Signed-off-by trailers for DCO checks are important habits when working with maintainers.

Code reviews are collaborative: Maintainer feedback is not criticism of your experience level—it is part of keeping a shared codebase accurate and consistent.

If you are a student or early-career developer interested in distributed systems and open source, you can start small and build momentum step by step:

Learn the core model first: Read the Dapr overview and documentation and test a small local application using one or two building blocks, such as State Management or Pub/Sub.

Follow structured courses: Explore Dapr University to understand how Dapr's building blocks, workflows, and agent patterns fit together.

Look for documentation and example issues: Check repositories such as dapr/docs or SDK repositories like dapr/js-sdk for unclear examples, outdated instructions, or small documentation fixes.

Read contribution guidelines before opening a PR: Check each repository's contribution guide so you follow commit formatting, branch naming, and DCO sign-off rules from the start.

Going from reading about distributed systems in university to contributing to Dapr's JavaScript SDK examples and documentation has been a meaningful part of my growth as a software engineering student at ITESCAM.

Open source does not require waiting until you know everything—it rewards curiosity, attention to detail, and willingness to collaborate.

If you want to explore Dapr and get involved, start with these official resources:

 The marketing industry is turning to artificial intelligence (AI) as a way to save time and execute smarter, more personalized campaigns. 61% of marketers say AI software is the most important aspect of their data strategy.

  If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

1. Jasper Ai(Formerly known as Jarvis)


Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Key Features

  •  It's trusted by 50,000+ marketers for creating engaging marketing campaigns, ad copy, blog posts, and articles within minutes which would traditionally take hours or days. Special Features:
  • Blog posts have been optimized for search engines and rank high on Google and other search engines. This is a huge plus for online businesses that want to generate traffic to their website through content marketing.
  • 99.9% Original Content and guarantees that all content it generates will be original, so businesses can focus on their online reputation rather than worrying about penalties from Google for duplicate content.
  • Long-Form Article Writing – Jasper.ai is also useful for long-form writing, allowing users to create articles of up to 10,000 words without any difficulty. This is ideal for businesses that want to produce in-depth content that will capture their audience’s attention.

The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Key Features

  • Identifies  top three interests based on metrics like time on page, recency, and frequency of each contact
  • Works with every ESP and CRM
  • Easy to get up and running in days
  • Enterprise-grade technology at a low cost for SMBs

3. Seventh Sense

  Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers 

Key Features 

  • AI determines the best send-time and email frequency for each contact
  • Connects with HubSpot and Marketo

4. Phrasee

  Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

Key Features 

  • Instantly generates millions of human-sounding, brand-compliant copy variants
  • Creates tailored language models for every customer
  • Learns what your audience responds to and rebuilds the prediction model every time

5. Hubspot Seo

  HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

Key Features 

  • Helps you discover and rank topics that people are searching for
  • Provides suggestions for your topic clusters and related subjects
  • Integrates with all other HubSpot content tools to help you create a well-rounded content strategy

 6. Evolve AI

  When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Key Features 

  • Figures out which content provides the best performance
  • Lets you test multiple ideas in a single experiment instead of having to perform many individual tests over a long period
  • Lets you try all your ideas across multiple pages for full-funnel optimization
  • Offers visual and code editors

7. Acrolinx

  Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

Key features

  • Reviews and scores existing content to ensure it meets your brand guidelines
  • Finds opportunities to improve your content and use automation to shorten your editorial process.
  • Integrates with more than 50 tools and platforms, including Google Docs, Microsoft Word, WordPress, and most web browsers.

8. MarketMuse 

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Key features:

  • The built-in editor shows how in-depth your topic is covered and what needs improvement
  • Finds gaps and opportunities for new content creation, prioritized by their probable impact and your chance of ranking

9. Copilot

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Key features: 

  • Integrate Facebook Messenger directly with your website, including chat history and recent interactions for a fluid customer service experience

  • Send branded images, promotional content, or coupon codes to those who opt in

  • Demonstrate social proof on your website with a widget, or push automatic Facebook posts sharing recent purchases
  • Display a promotional banner on your website to capture contacts instantly

10. Yotpo

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Key features:

  • Makes it easy for shoppers to filter reviews and find the exact information they’re looking for
  • Analyzes customer feedback and sentiments to help you improve your products
  • Integrates with most leading eCommerce platforms, including BigCommerce, Magento, and Shopify.

11. Albert AI

  Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

  Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

Key features:

  • Breaks down large amounts of data to help you customize campaigns
  • Plugs into your marketing technology stack and can be used across diverse media outlets, including email, content, paid media, and mobile

Final Saying

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9476. Practical Guide to Fine-Tuning Speech Models: From Data Cleaning to ASR/TTS Deployment (with Whisper, Fun-ASR, GPT-SoVITS)

General-purpose speech models work out of the box, but the moment they encounter industry jargon, regional accents, proprietary product names, or a fixed voice, they start "hallucinating" or going off-key. Fine-tuning isn't magic—it boils down to three core things: getting the data alignment clean, choosing the right freezing strategy, and紧盯 (keeping a close eye on) validation metrics. Below, we break it down in engineering deployment order, providing reproducible configurations for both ASR and TTS pipelines.

I. First, Clarify What You're Fine-Tuning

• ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition): Audio → Text. Representatives: Whisper, Fun-ASR-Nano, Qwen-Audio, etc.

• TTS / Voice Cloning (Speech Synthesis): Text + Reference Audio → Audio. Representatives: GPT-SoVITS, Qwen3-TTS, ChatTTS, VITS family.

• End-to-End Speech Large Models: Unified modeling of audio tokens ↔ text tokens. During fine-tuning, usually only the adapter or LLM intermediate layers are modified.

For model selection, don't jump straight to full-parameter fine-tuning. For <100 hours of domain data, prioritize LoRA / Adapter / only unfreezing the decoder; consider full-parameter tuning only when data exceeds 10,000 hours.

II. Data Preparation: Determines 80% of the Ceiling

ASR Data Checklist (JSONL or two-column CSV)

{"audio": "data/001.wav", "sr": 16000, "duration": 6.2, "text": "Send me the X7-Pro spec sheet via email", "domain": "erp_order", "speaker": "sp_023"}

Hard rules: • Unified 16 kHz mono. Use the model's built-in log_mel_spectrogram; don't calculate mel manually with librosa.

• Single clip ≤ 30 s (Whisper window); cut long audio at natural pauses.

• Trim leading/trailing silence, double-label + spot-check, manually verify alignment for 10 random clips—misalignment is more fatal than poor hyperparameters.

• Domain data : General data ≈ 7:3 mix, to prevent "forgetting how to speak."

• 10 hours is the starting point; 30+ hours brings a performance leap; for <10 hours, freeze the encoder and only train the decoder.

• 1–30 min of clean dry vocals per speaker for zero-shot trial; 1.5–3 hours of fine-tuning is needed to stably beat zero-shot similarity.

• Long audio → UVR to remove BGM → cut into 3–10 s segments → ASR for labeling → manual correction of typos (typos = voice drift).

• Annotation format: audio|speaker|lang|text, use zh/en/ja/ko/yue for lang.

• For speaker embedding, don't use a single reference clip; take the centroid of 64 embeddings, boosting cosine similarity from ~0.7 to 0.85+.

III. ASR Fine-Tuning: Two Paths — Whisper & Fun-ASR

model = WhisperForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained("openai/whisper-medium")

peft_config = LoraConfig(r=16, target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj"], lora_dropout=0.05, bias="none")

for p in model.model.encoder.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False

• lr: Full-parameter 1e-5, LoRA 1e-4; warmup 500–2000 steps + cosine decay

• bf16/fp16 + gradient checkpointing, effective batch 16–64 (use grad accum to reach)

• SpecAugment: use conservatively (don't mask too aggressively when domain data is scarce)

• Metrics: Validation set WER / CER, early stop if no drop for 3 consecutive epochs

• Vocabulary expansion: After adding new domain tokens to tokenizer, train embedding with a higher lr separately; don't let random initialization drag down convergence

Practical reference: 20h medical dictation fine-tuned on medium, terminology WER 12% → 4.5%; 4h Icelandic fine-tuned on turbo, 18% → 6%.

Path B: Fun-ASR-Nano (ChatML format, full-parameter friendly)

Convert data to ChatML: {"messages":[ {"role":"system","content":"You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role":"user","content":"Speech transcription:!./audio/001.wav"}, {"role":"assistant","content":"Order has generated a sales order"} ]}

Freezing strategy based on data volume: • <1000 h: Only train audio_adaptor

• <5000 h: Train audio_encoder + audio_adaptor

After training: run decode.py → whisper_mix_normalize.py for inverse normalization → compute-wer.

IV. TTS / Voice Cloning Fine-Tuning: GPT-SoVITS & Qwen3-TTS

GPT-SoVITS Pipeline (WebUI is the easiest)

Pitfalls: • OOM → Reduce batch size or enable is_half

• Metallic sound → Use v4 (native 48 kHz); v3 has upsampling artifacts

• One audio clip only learns one "speaking state"; if trained on singing, it will output singing

• Loss = talker loss (codebook 0) + 0.3 × sub-talker loss (layers 1–15)

• lr ≤ 1e-5, warmup + cosine; flat lr causes early overshooting and late overfitting

• Bake speaker embedding centroid into checkpoint; TTFA reduced from ~154 ms (ICL) to ~130 ms

Preventing Catastrophic Forgetting (Multi-speaker incremental training)

• Decouple speaker encoder, freeze backbone and only train embedding / adapter

• LoRA per-speaker stores matrices, without touching base weights

• Replay: Mix in 5–10% old speaker samples, or use generative pseudo-replay

V. Hyperparameter Quick Reference (Single A100/H100 starting point)

Item ASR Full-param ASR LoRA TTS Fine-tuning

Early Stop WER no drop WER no drop Similarity/MCD no rise

Optimizer unified as AdamW, weight_decay 0.01, grad clip 1.0.

ASR: WER/CER (look at by domain subcategory), terminology recall rate, long audio segmentation error rate. TTS: MOS (human 1–5), speaker similarity (SV system cos), MCD (lower is better), ASR-WER inverse test for intelligibility, RTF/TTFA.

With 1.5h of data fine-tuning Qwen3-TTS, it may not beat zero-shot in similarity/MOS, but it wins in "no need to carry reference audio every time" and more stable batch inference—this is the engineering value of fine-tuning.

• ASR: Export to ONNX / faster-whisper format, quantize to INT8 to compress size to 35%, accuracy drop <2%.

• TTS: Load voice packs independently, share main model as a singleton, switch via speaker_embedding.

• Mobile/Edge: TensorRT or MLC-LLM route, 10 MB-level adapter is more realistic than full model.

• Compliance: Must obtain authorization for real human voices, embed watermarks in synthetic audio, prohibit sensitive scenarios.

One-sentence conclusion: The deciding factor in speech fine-tuning isn't model size, but "10 hours of clean 16 kHz aligned domain data + correct layer freezing + WER/similarity early stopping." Hyperparameters merely cash in the data quality; no matter how fancy the LoRA, it can't save misaligned data.

#9473. S3 Security Defaults Changed. Have You Checked Your Older Buckets?

A new S3 bucket and a bucket created several years ago can sit in the same AWS account with different access settings. If your security review starts with a recently created bucket, it is worth checking what the older ones look like too.

In April 2023, Amazon S3 completed a rollout that enabled Block Public Access and disabled access control lists (ACLs) by default for newly created buckets. The announcement explicitly left existing buckets’ settings unchanged. AWS announcement · Rollout details

For teams maintaining long-running environments, that creates a useful review task. Check whether older buckets still depend on access arrangements that your current deployment templates have moved away from.

Start with an inventory across the AWS accounts you manage. Include buckets used for backups, exports, logs, and applications that have already been retired.

For each bucket, record its owner, purpose, current Block Public Access settings, Object Ownership setting, and any documented access exceptions. Compare those settings with your current infrastructure templates.

An older bucket may have a valid reason for its configuration. Give that reason an owner and a review date so the next person can understand it.

If you use the AWS CLI, these commands retrieve two useful parts of the bucket configuration:

These results are a starting point. A full access review also needs to consider account-level controls and the relevant policies.

With the Bucket owner enforced setting, ACLs are disabled and access is evaluated through policies. AWS recommends keeping ACLs disabled for most modern use cases. Existing workloads may still rely on ACL-based permissions, so review those dependencies before changing the setting. S3 Object Ownership documentation

Pay particular attention to applications that upload objects from another account and integrations that set an ACL during upload. Ask who writes the objects, who needs to read them, and how those permissions are currently granted.

AWS documents an approach using access logs and CloudTrail information to identify ACL-dependent requests and migrate their permissions to policies. Use that evidence alongside application testing when planning a change. AWS guide to identifying ACL dependencies

For a critical integration, rehearse both sides of the workflow. Confirm that the producer can upload an object and that the intended consumer can retrieve it.

Encryption has a different scope to the access-default changes.

Since January 5, 2023, S3 has automatically applied server-side encryption to new object uploads. The automatic baseline uses S3-managed keys, while existing customer-configured default encryption settings continue to apply. That rollout did not retroactively encrypt previously stored, unencrypted objects. S3 default encryption FAQ

If a bucket contains years of retained data, inspect the encryption status of those objects as part of the review. Also confirm whether your internal requirements call for a particular encryption configuration or key.

For a large collection, S3 Inventory can help you examine object metadata without manually opening objects one at a time. If historical objects need changes, plan the operation around retention requirements, application access, and the permissions required to read the resulting objects.

Choose one older bucket that supports an active application or recovery process.

Confirm its owner, review its access settings, and test the application workflow in an approved environment before scheduling any configuration change. Record what you found in the same place your team maintains the deployment configuration or runbook.

That gives the next review a clear starting point and helps explain why the bucket is configured the way it is.

Have you found an older S3 bucket whose permissions differed from your current deployment templates? What made the dependency difficult to trace?

#9464. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

#9461. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier

In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

#9450. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”
