#9393. The Absolute Best Pizza In Your State

There's probably no food more universally adored among Americans than pizza. Aside from being extremely customizable, every state has its own version of the best pizza — at least 15 distinct varieties and styles of making pizza can be found in the U.S. This makes it difficult to compare them. After all, the differences between a Detroit deep-dish and a chewy New Haven pie are many.

This list sets aside nationwide pizza chains and restaurants that happen to have pizza on the menu, and seeks to highlight the most delicious pizza in each state. We considered customer reviews from all over the internet, as well as any regional or national honors attributed to each pizza, and compared the overall cultural legacy and impact of each restaurant. What we ended up with was delicious pizza places that were worthy of being the best in each state. When a good frozen pizza (or even the best frozen pizzas) won't cut it, these are the spots to check out.

A well-traveled mainstay of Huntsville, Alabama, Valentina's Pizzeria has a reputation for serving New York-style pizza in a deep Southern atmosphere alongside other confections and dishes made in an Italian-American tradition. Joe Carlucci, the maestro behind Valentina's Pizzeria, is a co-founder of the World Pizza Champions organization, and his pizzeria is a local favorite — just check the comments on any of Valentina's Pizzeria's posts.

25783 Huntsville Brownsferry Rd, Madison, AL 35756

People love Moose's Tooth Pub & Pizzeria because it delivers on its goal of offering a "gourmet pizza experience, focusing on creative, quality food in a casual environment." The menu (with a robust list of temporary featured pizzas) reflects a creative urge to innovate. Moose's Tooth is the best-reviewed pizza in Alaska, according to Yelp and Google. There's no shortage of outdoor ambience in Alaska, so in addition to its indoor pub seating, Moose's Tooth offers outdoor, fireside seating for crisp days and nights.

Every pie at Via Della Slice Shop is crafted with artful attention to detail, and it's this skill and the friendly customer service that keep people coming back for more. Though a small and relatively simple operation, the restaurant is dedicated to making pizza of the highest quality; it proofs its dough for at least two days. According to Yelp, the vodka pizza is a particular favorite among returning customers, but Via Della is noted for its rotating flavors.

While DeLuca's Pizza has recently received accolades for its unconventional Spite Burger, it is best known for its brick-oven-baked pizza pies sold out of two locations in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Pizza influencer Dave Portnoy gave DeLuca's pizza an 8.7 out of 10, adding that it "blew [his] socks off [and] can compete with anybody in the country." And the non-influencers love it, too, with some people even driving multiple hours just to get a bite.

Tony's Pizza Napoletana was recognized this year as the No. 5 best pizzeria in the world, according to 50 Top Pizza. Tony's is just as popular with customers as with critics, as it's maintained a high star rating through tens of thousands of eviews on Google. Tony Gemigani — owner and 13-time World Pizza Champion — has spent years perfecting his pies; any West Coast pizza crawl would be incomplete without a visit to Tony's.

1570 Stockton St, San Francisco, CA 94133

Blue Pan Pizza offers delicious, Detroit-style pizza with a little bit of Denver flair. It's known for its Detroit-style pies, but it offers other versions and has been noted by folks for its tasty gluten-free options as well.

Detroit-style pizza is pan-baked pizza, and Blue Pan even serves to-go pies in rectangular, bright blue boxes made to look like its titular bakeware. Blue Pan was voted Readers' Choice for Best Denver Pizzeria by Denver Westword in 2024 and enjoys a huge local following.

A staple of Connecticut and specifically New Haven-style pizza since 1938, Sally's Apizza is a legendary spot amongst locals and pizza fanatics. New Haven-style pizza is made of high-hydration dough and cooked at a high heat in order to achieve a chewy, airy crust.

A new fan of Sally's wrote on Yelp, "It was a perfect meal, in a nice, cozy old school spot, that I'll definitely be craving until I'm back in town."

La Pizzeria Metro is a lovely little pizza place with two Delaware locations that offer a breezy, friendly dining experience and delicious pizza. Customers can even settle at the bar and tables with a view of pizza chefs at work.

La Pizzeria Metro's many specialty pizzas are named after landmark spots in Wilmington, an apt choice given how popular the place is with locals. One local reviewer wrote, "La Pizzeria Metro absolutely nails [creative pizza]. Their pizzas somehow manage to feel both authentic and wildly inventive."

It's no secret online that Florida's pizza options leave much to be desired. But Satchel's Pizza in Gainesville is a diamond in the rough.

It's a beloved destination for locals who praise both its delicious pizza and eclectic atmosphere. Some would even argue it's not just the best pizza in Florida; it might just be the best in the south. Even with thousands of reviews online, Satchel's maintains a very high star average rating.

Antico Pizza Napoletana is a pizzeria located in Atlanta's Little Italia. Founded by Giovanni "Gio" Di Palma, Antico offers only Neapolitan-style pizza cooked in wood-burning ovens, and thanks to its impeccable quality, earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand in 2023. The pizza is so good, in fact, that it earned the highest score out of all pizzerias reviewed in Zagat's first survey of pizza places in major U.S. cities.

Though Pizza Mamo only began selling pies in 2020, it's quickly been established as a neighborhood mainstay in Honolulu and has earned an Ilima Award — Hawaii's most prestigious restaurant recognition. Pizza Mamo's pies are based on a four-day fermented dough that provides a satisfying, chewy consistency in every slice. A local Yelp reviewer wrote, "Best pizza I've had on the island ... the pepperoni has a nice spice to it, and the dough is PERFECT."

Despite its remote location, Embers by the Lake has garnered tons of glowing online reviews – and the pizzeria's gorgeous lakeside backdrop is only a small part of what customers love. A great spot for family outings, Embers by the Lake has earned official recognition determined by customers, entities, and critics, including a local organization called North Idaho Life, which awarded it the first 5-Star Dining Destination Award.

12008 N Woodland Beach Dr, Hauser, ID 83854

Vito and Nick's Pizzeria is known for its Chicago tavern-style pies, which are made with a round, cracker-thin crust and cut into squares. It's a parlor that's been in business for more than 75 years and is an iconic institution to locals and tourists alike. The CBS Chicago Pizza Tournament awarded Vito and Nick's the grand prize in 2023, and the parlor has been positively featured on Food Network's "Diners, Drive-ins and Dives."

Tre Mori is much more than a pizza restaurant — the menu offers finely crafted pasta dishes and baked breads — but the pizza is definitely its signature. Dedicated to an old-style Italian sensibility, Tre Mori utilizes fresh and home-prepared ingredients, as well as supplies and foods imported from Italy (including the beautiful brick oven). On Yelp, Tre Mori is a top-100 US pizza joint, and on Onebite, it earns consistently positive reviews from customers.

8220 E 106th St Suite 200, Indianapolis, IN 46256

Fong's Pizza in Des Moines occupies the same space that once housed the oldest Chinese restaurant in America. As such, it offers a fusion of Chinese flavors and Italian fundamentals. Fong's claims to be the originator of the crab rangoon pizza (Alton Brown swears by it), and the restaurant earns great customer feedback for its fresh ingredients and timely service.

Even though Back Alley Pizza has only been operating for a little over 10 years, it has become a staple of Newton, Kansas, and a magnet for regional recognition. On Yelp, satisfied customers rejoice over the best pizza they've ever had, period. Though Back Alley Pizza doesn't claim a signature "style" of pizza, it does tout its original BBQ pizza as a signature. But you'll be happy with any slice you try.

Miguel's Pizza feels like a well-loved small business with a dedicated following and a commitment to capturing Kentucky's rustic charm in combination with a warm, friendly atmosphere. Pizza Today has featured Miguel's as a must-stop destination, and many recognize the pizzeria as a key element in the economic development of Kentucky's Red River Gorge. All of that is because of the quality of the pizza, which people just can't get enough of.

Zander White, founder of Zee's Pizzeria, pursued pizza-making as a hobby until the COVID-19 pandemic, during which he had to find a new way to support his family. White was so successful selling pies from his kitchen that he opened Zee's Pizzeria, which was named one of the top pizza places in New Orleans by Gambit Weekly. Customers appreciate the thin crust, sweet sauce, and classic taste.

The purveyors at Brickyard Hollow Brewing Company (which began in Yarmouth) realized that few things pair better with a glass of craft beer than a slice of craft pizza, which has become as much of a draw as the beer – if not more so.

Brickyard Hollow has a greater mission to provide fun and comfort to local Maine communities and residents looking to connect more closely with their neighbors. It's received rave reviews from local critics and is rapidly expanding thanks to overwhelming regional support.

In December 2024, Barstool pizza reviewer Dave Portnoy stopped by TinyBrickOven to do a quick slice review. He gave TinyBrickOven's pizza a 7.9/10 rating and $60,000 to turn the small business big. It was that good. TinyBrickOven is a staple of Baltimore, with local customers and other supporters even accepting the owner's self-anointed title, "the Michael Jordan of pizza."

Widely regarded as Boston's oldest operating pizza place, Regina Pizzeria has been serving slices and pies around Boston's North End since 1926. The quality comes from an impeccable dough — chewy yet crisp and perfectly charred — that's baked inside a 900-degree gas-fired oven. Boston Magazine calls it one of the city's best, and in 2018, Tripadvisor named Regina Pizzeria the best in the nation. Taste of Massachusetts included it in its list of top 11 favorite pizzas in the state.

In 2024, Yelp named Loui's Pizza in Hazel Park, Michigan, as the best pizza spot in the Midwest. It's been family-owned since 1977, and for nearly half a century, it's been pumping out top-tier Detroit-style pies that are chewy, crisp, cheesy, and properly sauced. The Detroit Metro Times ranked Loui's as the No. 1 Detroit-style pizza in the area, citing its "tangy sauce, crispy caramelized edges, and an abundance of cheese" as a few of the reasons why this pizza stands out.

When you have the endorsement from global food aficionado Andrew Zimmern, you know you're doing something right. Punch Pizza is the people's pizzeria, a beloved St. Paul institution that has now expanded to 12 locations. It specializes in Neapolitan-style pizza, cooked for about a minute and a half in a scorching-hot, wood-burning oven. It has earned numerous awards and recognitions, including a Quality Business Award in 2025.

Leña Pizza + Bagels is giving Mississippi some long-deserved culinary attention. Chef and owner Marisol Doyle grew up in Mexico, moved to Mississippi, and studied pizza making in Naples, Italy. The restaurant was quickly named one of the best in the United States by both the New York Times and the prestigious Italian pizza review board, 50 Top Pizza. However, the biggest honor came in 2024, when Doyle was named one of the top 100 pizza chefs in the world.

You've heard of New York-, New Haven-, and Detroit-style pizza, but — unless you're from Missouri, you probably aren't familiar with St. Louis-style pies. And Pirrone's Pizzeria, which has been around since 1976, arguably makes the best one in the state. The rectangular dough is crisp and cracker-thin and covered in melted Provel, a triple-blend processed cheese invented in St. Louis.

Eugene's Pizza has remained a community staple for over 60 years. In 2015 and 2016, it was the back-to-back champion of the Montana Mint pizza bracket, and in 2026, Reader's Digest recognized the pizzeria as the best in Montana. Eugene's serves some wild pies, with topping options ranging from taco-seasoned ground beef and sauerkraut to shrimp and mandarin oranges.

Founded in 1919 by World War I veteran Alfonso Orsi, the bakery and pizzeria has racked up thousands of excellent reviews on Google. Its near-perfect score has a lot to do with its pizza dough — prepared fresh in small batches every morning using a simple recipe of yeast, salt, water, and high-gluten wheat flour. Tripadvisor ranks it the top pizzeria in Omaha, and our sister site, Mashed, listed it as the best Italian restaurant in Nebraska.

Red Dwarf is a triumvirate of pleasures: it's a pizzeria, rum-infused Tiki party, and rock show all in one. The Detroit-style pies have a "crispy edge [and an] airy center" and are loaded with topping combinations that include everything from brown sugar-glazed ham, pineapple, and jalapeño to mushrooms, peppers, and garlic creme sauce. In 2025, Red Dwarf won the Reader's Choice Best Pizza Award from Las Vegas Weekly, and commenters on Facebook, Reddit, and Google agree it's the best pizza in town.

1305 Vegas Valley Dr, Las Vegas, NV 89169

In New England, New Haven-style pizza gets all the attention, but venture a few hundred miles north, and you'll find another popular regional variety: Greek-style. With these pies, the dough bakes in a high-walled pan that's generously coated with olive oil to achieve an extra-crisp, almost fried bottom crust. And few places execute it better than New Hampshire's Tilton House of Pizza. It appears on roundups as the best pizza place in New Hampshire and has a near-perfect rating on Google.

New Jersey certainly takes its pizza seriously. Part of that reputation can be attributed to the De Lorenzo family, who opened their first New Jersey restaurant in 1936. In 2021, Food and Wine recognized New Jersey as the best state for pizza in the country, calling out De Lorenzo's specifically as "one of the finest classic pies in the entire Northeast." Its namesake tomato pie is hand-stretched, layered with cheese — then sauce — and baked until charred.

According to the Albuquerque Journal, Pizza Barn is slinging some of the best pies in all of New Mexico. And any pizzeria with a fireplace and a drive-thru deserves special recognition. Pizza Barn is known for its roasted green chiles — a popular condiment throughout the state — which it liberally scatters over its pies and breadsticks.

John's of Bleecker, the famed no-slice pizzeria, has been blazing dough in its coal-fired oven since 1929. The pies are thin, crisp, and beautifully blistered, topped with a just-sweet-enough tomato sauce, and then baked fast and hot. With Google reviewers praising its old-school traditions, service, and the pizza itself, this is one of the most respected New York City pizzerias — if not the world.

Oakwood Pizza Box anchors the pizza scene in the North Carolina Research Triangle. It was awarded Best Pizza in 2026 by Midtown Magazine, a publication that highlights life in the greater Raleigh area. It serves an excellent Northeastern-style pizza: thin, foldable, cheesy, and not overly sauced. Its square pies are about the size of a large pillowcase and can be ordered with a sesame seed crust.

North Dakota has carved out its own style of pizza, which is heartier than your average Neapolitan pie or New York-style slice. Since the early 2000s, Rhombus Guys have been baking doughy, tire-sized pizzas that have earned it the reputation as one of the best (and most inventive) pizzerias in the state. The restaurant's signature T-Rex pizza — a hulking combination of pepperoni, sausage, and other toppings — won the Grand Forks People's Choice competition six years in a row.

Rarely do you see such a consensus on Reddit and Facebook, but when it comes to Il Rione, almost everyone agrees that it makes one of the best pies in Cleveland — if not the state. It serves a gorgeous New York-style pizza that, in 2025, beat out 32 other pizzerias to win the title of Best Pizza in the Land from the local media outlet I'm From Cleveland. It's also a favorite of Iron Chef (and Cleveland native) Michael Symon.

Most of the pizzerias on this list are primarily standalone restaurants. Hideaway is one of the few exceptions, with 27 locations across three states. In 1957, its original location opened in Stillwater, next to the Oklahoma State University campus. With pizza names like Pepperonipalooza and Aporkalypse, it's no surprise that The New York Times listed it as one of 15 of its readers' favorite pizza places from around the world.

At Lovely's Fifty Fifty,  chef/co-owner Sarah Minnick uses her art degree to craft her stunning edible mosaics. Her sourdough starter, local grains, flowers, and seasonal ingredients help her pizza achieve an inimitable tang and toothsome chew. With write-ups in Portland Monthly, a feature in Food & Wine, and an impressive 9.0 score from the Infatuation, Lovely's has become one of the most respected pizzerias in the country.

4039 N Mississippi Ave, Portland, OR 97217

Opened in 1924, the Corropolese Italian Bakery & Deli is most famous for its tomato pie: a sturdy, cake-like dough covered in smooth tomato sauce, sprinkled with a light dusting of Romano cheese, and served at room temperature. Over the century, it has become a cornerstone of Philadelphia food culture, so much so that in 2023, Corropolese's won Herr's second annual #FlavoredbyPhilly contest. The prize? A Herr's chip flavor inspired by its famous tomato pie.

For such a tiny state, Rhode Island has plenty of quality pizzerias, but one that keeps showing up on lists of local favorites is Pasquale's. With a treasured Associazione Vera Pizza Napoletana certification, it's no surprise the pizzeria has earned so many accolades. In 2025, 50 Top Pizza named it the 12th best in the U.S., and Rhode Island Monthly magazine acknowledges it as one of the state's great pizzerias.

59 S County Commons Way, Wakefield, RI 02879

Four years later, D'Allesandro's was one of three pizzerias to win the title of Best Pizza Joint from The Guide to South Carolina. Eater followed suit in 2025, featuring D'Alessandro's on its list of the 13 best stops for pizza in Charleston.

Opened in 1959, Charlie's Pizza House is the oldest pizzeria in South Dakota. Its lineup of eclectic specialty pizzas, with names like "Hepburn's Spicy Delight," "John Wayne's BBQ Style," and "Marilyn's Mermaid Heaven," which is topped with shrimp, crab, and green and black olives, honors Hollywood stars of past decades. The restaurant has also received national acclaim, with the Food Network naming Charlie's South Dakota's best pizza place.

A Dopo is a wood-fired pizzeria in downtown Knoxville that has won over the hearts of residents and college students with its sourdough Neapolitan-style pizzas. The dinner-only pizzeria stepped into the national spotlight after making the list of USA Today's 2025 Restaurants of the Year, and it continues to rack up recognition, most recently receiving a nod from the Michelin Guide in 2026.

Cane Rosso is a pizzeria that has blossomed into nine locations across Texas. Its wood-fired pizzas are all 14 inches and baked in a blazing-hot oven, giving each pie its "signature leopard-spotted crust." Its toppings — beef brisket, bacon marmalade, smoked mozzarella, habanero honey — have a distinct Texas flair. In 2021, Food & Wine named it one of the best pizzerias in Texas, and it has since maintained its reputation for excellence.

The Pie Underground's flagship location, open since 1980, is the most beloved of its dozens of locations — just a stone's throw from the University of Utah campus. Folino's embodies the ethos of pizza artistry. Its naturally leavened dough uses a 14- year-old starter culture and is cold-proofed for three days to achieve a one-of-a-kind crust that's light, layered, and intentionally tangy. Dr. Ho's describes itself as "the alternative pizza." And we can't help but agree. The Carlson Block is a destination restaurant, nestled cozily in Wilkeson, a tiny coal-mining town. The Seattle Times featured the pizzeria, asking rhetorically if it's making the best pizza in the state. House-made mozzarella, seasonal ingredients, a deft hand, and a commitment to the craft ensure Carlson Block will remain among the state's best pizza places.

You know what you're getting at Pies & Pints: quality draft beer and fiercely innovative pizzas. It's an endless list, which means you'll just have to come back again and again to try them all, as many West Virginia residents have been doing.

Open for over a century, Wells Brothers serves a handful of Italian classics, but it's most famous for its pizzas. A relative newcomer, Bella Fuoco is wowing with its blistered, wood-fired pizzas. Determining the "best" pizza is largely subjective. For states with a distinct regional variation, we selected shops that are an excellent representation of that style. We also considered restaurants that have stood the test of time or are pillars of the community, and placed weight on glowing social media reviews and awards. Overall customer experience was also considered, as was the impact on the home state's pizza culture.

#9391. Make A Reuben Upside Down-Style For More Caramelized Flavor

The origins of the Reuben are disputed, with some saying that it was invented in Nebraska while others insist that it is a New York original. Regardless of where you think this iconic sandwich was born, the combination of corned beef, cheese, sauerkraut, and Russian dressing (or Thousand Island dressing) on rye bread is something that few people mess with. The method for making it also tends to remain unchanged, with many restaurants and home cooks pressing it in a sandwich press or skillet. This is just fine for the traditional recipe, but if you want to give your Reuben a layer of caramelized flavor, you're going to need to shake up tradition just a little bit by making it upside down-style. Instead of building your sandwich starting with the bread, start with the cheese touching the pan or baking sheet.

Cheeses like Swiss, which is the preferred kind for making a classic Reuben sandwich recipe, contain proteins and a little bit of sugar in the form of lactose. It's these two elements that react to the direct heat of the pan to create the Maillard reaction, which is when food gets browned, developing complex flavors that make it irresistibly delicious. This contributes to a caramelized note in your sandwich and echoes the toasty notes of the bread. By adding additional cheese between the layers of meat, you ensure that there is a melty element as well. Adding the kraut right before assembling the final product prevents the moisture from getting in the way of browning.

Since the cheese is coming into direct contact with the cooking surface, you're going to need to ensure that it doesn't stick to whatever you're using to make your sandwich. If you're opting to make your Reuben on the stovetop, you're going to want to use a nonstick pan. Make sure it's hot, too, as this can also help prevent food from sticking. You're also going to want to use a thin, wide spatula that you can easily slide between the cheese and the pan to flip your sandwich halves so that you can toast the bread.

If you're choosing to bake your Reuben upside down-style, be sure to use Ina Garten's favorite thing to line a sheet pan: parchment paper, which you can easily peel away from the toasted cheese after flipping your sandwich halves over. You'll also want to ensure you're baking your sandwiches at the right temperature to get both the cheese and bread toasted and crisp, and 375 degrees Fahrenheit is typically ideal.

Regardless of which method you choose, you should always spread some kind of fat on your bread for even more flavor, and this is something you can play around with without breaking from tradition too much. Butter or mayonnaise are typically used in toasted sandwiches, but you can also opt for ghee, which has a nuttier flavor. Bacon fat is also an intensely flavorful alternative, but if you want to mirror the meatiness of the corned beef, go for beef tallow.

#9390. The 7 Most Common Mistakes Home Cooks Make When Cooking Mashed Potatoes

The simplest Thanksgiving side deserves better.

In a traditional Thanksgiving meal, mashed potatoes are a seemingly simple side dish that does a lot of heavy lifting. They're the perfect vessel for a puddle of gravy, and they’re a creamy complement to everything else on your plate—yes, even your aunt's questionable green bean casserole.

Mashed potatoes prove you can transform even the humblest ingredients into something magical. And yet, we've all somehow still eaten bad ones. With a recipe this basic, even the smallest mistakes have nowhere to hide.

Thankfully, those mistakes are 100% avoidable. We rounded up the most common ways to mess up mashed potatoes so that yours turn out as delicious as possible this holiday season.

It doesn’t matter if you cut your potatoes into a fine dice or rough chunks. Whatever size you pick, stick with it. Making sure your potato pieces are roughly the same size will help them all cook at the same rate. If your knife work is haphazard, you may end up with some pieces that are perfectly cooked, others that are waterlogged and mushy, and some that are still firm in the center.

Like pasta, potatoes need a good amount of seasoning to really shine—which is why salting the cooking water is so important. You can be generous with the salt, since much of it stays in the water and ends up going down the drain. When you start seasoning early in the cooking process, it’s easier to build flavor and adjust as you go.

In the hustle of cooking all of your Thanksgiving dishes, you may be tempted to boil your potatoes ahead of time and mash them later in the day. But it’s always better to work with potatoes while they’re still hot and easier to mash. Waiting until they’re cool will likely require far more elbow grease—and you’ll still end up with uneven chunks.

A smooth, creamy mash is the height of decadence. To make sure the potatoes are lump-free, some people may reach for a blender—but this is one of the most consequential mistakes you can make. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and the more you work them, the more starch gets released from their cell walls. Breaking out the blender may be well-intentioned, but it can leave you with potatoes that are gummy and gluey. Instead, opt for the right tool, like a hand masher, food mill, or potato ricer.

Another important thing to consider is that potato starches continue absorbing moisture as mashed potatoes sit. They can soak up the milk you’ve added, leaving your potatoes dry and dense. Don’t be afraid to add more liquid—or at least keep some extra on hand to loosen up your mash before serving.

Anthony Bourdain famously pointed to generous amounts of salt and butter as part of what makes restaurant food taste so good. That’s especially true for mashed potatoes. You may be scared to add more than a light sprinkle of salt, but don’t forget to taste and adjust the seasoning before serving. A little extra salt can make all the difference for your Thanksgiving dinner.

Whether you’re feeding your immediate family or a small army, you should always make a big batch of mashed potatoes. This side is one of the most popular components of a Thanksgiving menu, so it never hurts to make extra. It’s also one of the most versatile dishes for repurposing leftovers. You can transform them into gnocchi, shepherd’s pie, or crispy fried croquettes. It may require more mashing in the moment, but your future self will thank you.

#9388. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9387. 5 Reasons You Shouldn't Get Costco Delivered

A Costco membership is like a real-life, grown-up golden ticket, your passport to bulk-buy deals and steals, as well as its incomparable food court, including the hands-down best menu item, the hot dog and soda combo. It's a terrific shopping option, especially when you have a large family or you're shopping to feed a lot of mouths, as for a party or holiday gathering. While Costco does want to encourage its shoppers to come into its stores and take a look around (and perhaps buy a few things off-the-cuff), the major warehouse chain has also partnered with third-party shopping apps to offer same-day delivery of its goods. But it might not be the best option when you need your Costco fix.

Starting in 2017 with limited availability through Instacart, and now expanding to almost the entire country in 2026 with Uber Eats and DoorDash, Costco's delivery definitely has its positives, but the program isn't without its pitfalls, too. From higher prices to unpredictable delivery times, we're going to highlight several reasons you should maybe think twice before having Costco groceries delivered so that you can weigh your options and make the best decision for yourself.

While Costco's delivery option does allow nonmembers to shop at the warehouse, the company charges higher prices for most items ordered through the apps, helping offset delivery-related costs. And then there is the actual cost of the deliveries themselves, service fees, plus tips for the drivers, to the point where you might pay as much as 30% to 40% more than if you just shopped in-store.

If you've ever ordered takeout through DoorDash or Uber Eats, or groceries through Instacart, you might have found that the actual delivery took place long after the original drop-off time you were quoted. And the same thing can happen with Costco same-day delivery, which is a major pitfall if you have company coming over by a certain time and you need to prepare dinner or snacks.

When you are particular about your produce or search through packages of meat until you find just the right size and price, you might want to think twice about having your Costco order delivered. That's because you have to surrender nearly all control over what goes into your cart (though you can leave notes and instructions for your shoppers), and some shoppers are more careful, considerate, and, well, competent than others.

Most items that are available in stores will be visible and available for purchase through apps like Instacart and Uber Eats for same-day delivery. But it's worth noting that Costco also offers two-day delivery, and you may find favorite items missing from its selection. Redditors theorize this may be because the two-day delivery items are sourced from Costco Business Centers, which carry slightly different products.

Finally, Costco also delivers large appliances, so if you're weighing the pros and cons of buying a refrigerator through the warehouse chain, just know that some customers on Reddit have reported miscommunication, sometimes over information as basic as the delivery date, with one user even calling the experience "a nightmare."

It’s getting increasingly difficult to keep up with all the limited-edition tumblers, advent calendars, and seasonal releases that disappear off shelves before you’ve finished your morning coffee. And now IHOP is giving breakfast lovers another reason to make room in their kitchen cabinets.

IHOP says coffee is its second best-selling menu item, which means an awful lot of people have spent their mornings clutching one of those mugs while waiting for breakfast. But before you start planning an entire IHOP-themed kitchen makeover, know that each participating location will have just 24 (yes, only 24!) mugs available. Once they're gone, they’re gone, at least as far as this limited-time release is concerned.

There's certainly no shortage of things to collect this holiday season, but at least this one’s something you can actually put to use while doing some damage to a stack of pancakes.

#9384. Skip Potatoes: Make Beef Stew 100% More Delicious With An Ingredient From The Frozen Aisle

Potatoes are almost as important to beef stew as the meat itself. But when you substitute them with pierogi, you aren't necessarily removing the tuber so much as transforming its shape and making it 100% more delicious with a variety of other fillings.

Pierogi are European-style dumplings that you can stuff with everything from chicken to sauerkraut. Still, potato-based fillings are by far the most common, thanks to the delicious combination of a tender wrapping and rich, buttery center that freezes quite well. Making a sort of dumpling soup is one of the best ways to upgrade frozen pierogi, suffusing the dough with an incredibly savory beefiness that's almost impossible to replicate. But it also levels up your stew because you're essentially adding little pockets of mashed potatoes that won't dissipate into the broth!

This is an especially fantastic trick if you don't have much meat to begin with, bulking up your stew quite inexpensively. It's also a way to add ingredients that may not usually make their way into your recipe. Melting cheese directly into the pot may mess up the texture, but contained quantities of cheesy potatoes taste amazing when paired with an umami- and herb-rich broth. The best frozen pierogi brands also come with plenty of their own seasoning, so while bites of the dumplings will have an intense flavor, they won't overseason your stew directly unless you boil them so long that the wrapping breaks.

Beef stew typically needs to cook for at least a couple of hours to develop flavors and tenderize the ingredients. If you add pierogi right away, you run the risk of overboiling the dumplings and making them fall apart. Whether you drop them into the pot to let the wrappings absorb flavor or prepare them separately, timing is critical to preserving their texture.

If you plan on adding pierogi directly to the stew, it's best to leave them frozen. This allows the wrapping to absorb flavorful broth as the filling thaws. In a pot already at a simmer, 10 minutes should be all you need to ensure everything is heated through. If you use mini versions instead of full-size ones, you may want to cut this down to five minutes — when in doubt, follow package instructions. You can always add a lid and let the residual heat warm them through, but these are much easier to overcook.

Pan-frying pierogi first, then using them as a topping, can be a great way to add a more diverse range of flavors. Properly browned dough not only has a great depth of flavor, but also tends to stand up better against liquids and won't become soggy as quickly. This is especially good for leftovers since you can store your stew and dumplings separately so they won't become oversaturated in the fridge. Frying them up in butter can also add a bit of needed fat if you use a particularly lean cut of meat, making your stew richer.

#9382. This Thanksgiving, make your pies mini: Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

What’s the one food you most look forward to at Thanksgiving?

For some it’s the turkey. For others it’s the array of sides. But for many of us bakers, let’s admit it — our thoughts skip right over the apps and main meal and go straight to the pies, whether it's apple, pumpkin, pecan, or all of them together.

The problem is that for smaller gatherings, the need for multiple pies diminishes. Still, how can you bear to choose between apple, pumpkin, and pecan?

Enter the mini pie, a great way to showcase an array of pies and have them all disappear by the end of the day.

Here’s a potential hosting scenario this year: You’re serving six close family members (including yourself) at Thanksgiving dinner; you want to offer pumpkin, apple, and pecan pie. So you pull out your mini muffin pan and use it to make mini pies in a variety of different flavors. Everyone can enjoy one mini pie immediately, one later, and squirrel one away for the next day.

And mini pies aren't just handy for smaller gatherings — they can also make life a little easier during the frenetic rush of food prep in the days before Turkey Day. Helpfully, you can make these pies well ahead of Thanksgiving; they can be prepared, baked, and then frozen for up to a few weeks before serving.

Once cool, wrap each pie individually in plastic, then bag them all airtight and freeze. When you’re ready to serve, unwrap, thaw, and reheat briefly: 5 to 10 minutes in a 350°F oven or about 20 seconds (per pie) in a microwave will bring them back to life.

Because these mini pies have a higher crust-to-filling ratio, you don't need to prebake the crust to avoid a soggy bottom. Just place the pie dough rounds in your mini muffin pan, fill with about a tablespoon of the pumpkin custard, and bake.

Another benefit: The smaller amount of filling makes it easier to nail the bake. You don't have to look for a perfect amount of jiggle in your pie before removing from the oven — just bake until the exposed edges are golden brown and the custard is set in the center.

Turn to our Pecan Tassies recipe — a beloved Southern dessert, pecan tassies are basically just bite-size pecan pies. This recipe uses a tender, unsweetened cream cheese pastry, which cradles a gooey nut filling sweetened with brown sugar (no corn syrup).

We’ve saved perhaps the most beloved pie for last: apple. These mini apple pies are a bit more involved than the pumpkin or pecan pies. You need to precook the filling, and you have to choose how to top them. That said, they’re totally worth the effort (and the filling can be prepared up to five days in advance; store the cooled filling, covered, in the refrigerator until ready to bake).

Once you've precooked the diced apple filling on the stovetop to remove excess liquid, assemble your pies in your mini muffin pan by lining with rounds of pie dough and adding the apples. You can then choose how to top them:

You may be questioning whether making mini Thanksgiving pies is more trouble than it's worth. But helpfully, the techniques involved are very approachable — mix, roll, fill, bake — and the resulting pies are both delicious and just plain fun. Have you ever wanted a whole Thanksgiving pie just for yourself? You can have it — in miniature. Happy baking!

Do you say you won't dare bake pie because you're unsure of your skills with a rolling pin? Check out these other easy no-roll crusts: No-Roll Pie Crust and Graham Cracker Crust.

#9381. This Classic Italian Sandwich Is Extra Crispy & Delicious

Everybody celebrates Italy for pizza, pasta, and gelato, and while they're classics for a reason, we implore you to explore Italy's unrivaled gastronomic tapestry a little deeper. Trust us, there are some serious gems hidden just beneath the surface. One of our favorite Italian street foods that you need to try is porchetta, Italy's answer to crispy pork belly. Irresistibly crunchy and bursting with indulgent flavors, it makes for a seriously delicious sandwich filler.

Porchetta is a style of pork roast, but is completely unique in its preparation. It's typically made from a whole deboned pig or a large cut of pork belly, which is laid flat and heavily rubbed on the inside with salt, garlic, and black pepper, alongside quintessential Italian seasonings like rosemary, sage, and fennel seeds. The pork is then rolled back together and slow-roasted for several hours, allowing the interior to turn soft and tender while the skin develops a beautiful crackling.

Porchetta is a meal in itself, but goes even better in a sandwich. Start out with a thick Italian white bread, something that won't turn soggy when paired with the pork's rich meat juices and sauces — ciabatta or focaccia work perfectly here. To balance the richness, add something bright with a little zing. We think salsa verde is an excellent choice, since the lemon juice and vinegar bring a sharp acidity, while fresh parsley keeps the heavy roast from feeling cloying — it pairs perfectly with a Cuban interpretation of the recipe as well. Rather than piling on thick slabs of porchetta, slice it thinly, so it stays tender and folds nearly into the bread, and make sure every sandwich gets a few pieces of the crackling skin for a satisfying crunch. As for what else to put on the sandwich, draw inspiration from Bobby Flay's favorite Roman porchetta sandwich.

You should have no problem finding pre-rolled porchetta at the butcher, but why not save your money and make it at home instead? We promise it's not as intimidating as it looks. For the juiciest cut that's also easiest to roll and inexpensive, pick up a skin-on pork belly. Its exceptionally high fat content keeps the roast moist and makes it incredibly forgiving to work with, so even the least confident cooks won't have to worry about overcooking it.

Porchetta is the star of the sandwich, and it's the crackling skin that really steals the show, so getting it earth-shatteringly crispy is essential. Here, the secret to a crunchy crust is dryness, so before you get to work on seasoning, leave the pork uncovered in the fridge overnight to let the surface dry out. Many cooks also salt the meat generously before its rest, which draws out even more moisture. And before roasting, it's good practice to pat the skin completely dry, since any lingering moisture turns to steam and keeps the skin from crisping.

To keep the sandwich from turning into a soggy mess, it's essential to let your porchetta rest for around 15 to 30 minutes after roasting. It might be tempting to carve it right away and admire your hard work, but slicing too soon sends the flavorful juices flooding into the chopping board and then straight into the bread, which even the sturdiest ciabatta can't hold back. The logic is the same as with steak because resting gives the juices time to redistribute through the muscle, leaving the meat deliciously tender and flavorful.

#9380. People Are Calling The Day Before Thanksgiving ‘Green Wednesday’—And It’s Becoming A Huge Holiday

The turkey isn’t the only thing getting roasted.

Thanksgiving is known for plenty of traditions, from arguing over who makes the best mac and cheese to fighting for the last slice of pie. But there’s another tradition that's becoming increasingly popular.

If you've ever been at Thanksgiving dinner when a group of cousins suddenly announces they're going for a walk, you probably know what's happening. The so-called “cousin walk,” when relatives sneak away to smoke weed, has become such a recognizable holiday ritual that it's now inspiring TikTok videos, memes, and an entire shopping event.

Enter Green Wednesday, the cannabis industry’s answer to Black Friday.

Green Wednesday is the day before Thanksgiving, and it has become one of the year’s biggest shopping days for cannabis retailers. This year, it falls on November 25.

The term has been around since at least 2016, when cannabis delivery company Eaze began using it after noticing a surge in purchases ahead of Thanksgiving.

According to MJBizDaily, cannabis retailers recorded approximately $138.5 million in sales on Green Wednesday in 2025, up from $132.4 million the previous year, based on data from cannabis market intelligence company BDSA.

While Green Wednesday is often described as the industry’s second-biggest shopping day behind 4/20, some retailers are seeing even stronger results.

According to data RISE Dispensaries shared with Delish, Green Wednesday was its biggest sales day of 2025 and outperformed the notorious cannabis holiday 4/20. The company’s sales were roughly double an average Wednesday, while pre-rolls saw their strongest sales day of the year.

A major part of Green Wednesday’s cultural appeal comes from the infamous cousin walk—the tradition has become a recurring joke across social media, with TikTok users sharing videos about coordinating their annual walkabout. And, of course, brands are getting involved, too.

As Morning Brew reported, Jif referenced cousin walks in an Instagram promotion last year, while a Taco Bell and Hidden Valley collaboration played on a similar holiday joke. Cannabis brand Dogwalkers is also leaning into the tradition with a Cousin Walk Kit tied to Thanksgiving.

And while Green Wednesday and the cousin walk go hand in hand, cannabis use isn't limited to just the cousins.

A 2026 study from UC San Diego found that approximately 8.9% of Americans ages 65 and older had used cannabis in the previous year. Among those users, 40.5% reported consuming cannabis through food or drinks. Meanwhile, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration found that 22.4% of American adults used cannabis in 2025.

Americans’ drinking habits are changing, too. A 2026 Gallup survey found that just 54% of U.S. adults consume alcohol, down from 62% in 2023. While the figures don't establish that people are replacing alcohol with cannabis, they reflect changing consumption habits. It seems people are increasingly opting out of Blackout Wednesday and opting into Green Wednesday.

The growing conversation around edibles also comes with an important reminder: Cannabis-infused foods and drinks can take longer to produce noticeable effects than inhaled cannabis, and they should always be clearly labeled and kept away from children.

Between the sales numbers, viral cousin-walk jokes, and brands embracing the tradition, Green Wednesday is becoming a recognizable part of the Thanksgiving season. So when someone inevitably asks whether anyone wants to go for a walk after dinner, just know that an entire industry has been preparing for that moment.

#9377. Make Your Burgers Juicier With One Creamy Ingredient (Hint: It's Not Butter Or Milk)

There are a million ways to make patties juicier, from mixing in grated butter to even marinating your burgers. But if you're looking for something a bit outside the box that doesn't complicate the recipe too much, stuffing the patties with Velveeta can give you some seriously cheesy, moisture-rich results.

While it may sound odd, this recipe is actually a variation of a Juicy Lucy cheeseburger, a Minnesota staple dating back to the 1950s. The idea is that by trapping Velveeta between two thin patties, the cheese melts into a liquid center that mingles with the rendered meat juices, adding moisture to every bite. If done correctly, the cheese should settle back into a gooey state while the patties rest, helping ensure that you don't burn your mouth on molten dairy on your first bite.

While you can always stuff your burgers with other cheeses, Velveeta has one major advantage. Thanks to its emulsifying and stabilizing agents, it's less likely to become greasy as it melts. Other meltable cheeses can release fat as they heat up, which isn't a problem when it can drip onto a grill but can create problems when you leave it no room to escape. Plus, the fact that Velveeta comes in blocks makes it extremely easy to shape to fit your patties, no matter how large or small you prefer them.

The classic Juicy Lucy burger may seem a little daunting, but the process is actually quite simple. Trapping the cheese between the patties and ensuring that all your ingredients and, more importantly, your grill are at the right temperatures are all you really need to worry about for something crisp, delicious, and juicy.

Starting with one part Velveeta to four parts beef is your best bet for this recipe. It's enough cheese to achieve that gooey center but not so much that it'll escape and ruin the integrity of your patties. It's also best to keep your patties flat rather than thick, which makes it much easier to pinch the seams and trap the Velveeta between them. Velveeta is easier to work with when cold, but keeping your beef cold is also a major benefit for your burger. Cold beef fat is less likely to smear and instead stays in little pockets that help keep the meat even juicier.

Grilling your burgers at the right temperature helps you achieve a good crust without excessive moisture loss, and it's doubly important when you stuff the patties. You want enough heat to char the exterior but not so much that the patties finish cooking before your Velveeta has the chance to melt. Around 400 degrees Fahrenheit is a good sweet spot. It may be useful to keep one side of your grill cool, letting indirect heat finish any patties whose exteriors have cooked too quickly.

Before comparing your balance to anyone else's, you need to know what the benchmarks actually include. Most retirement savings data from Vanguard, Fidelity, and the Federal Reserve covers:

What these numbers typically exclude: taxable brokerage accounts, real estate equity, HSA balances invested for retirement, pension values, and Social Security. For FI-minded savers, this distinction matters enormously — your total investable net worth is almost certainly larger than your "retirement savings" as defined by these surveys.

The gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most important distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. The median (the middle number when all balances are ranked) gives you a far more honest picture of what a typical American actually has saved.

Notice how the gap widens with age. By 65+, the average is 3.3 times the median — meaning a small number of disciplined savers (or high earners) are pulling the average far above what most people actually have. The median tells you what a typical person in each age group actually holds. If you are above the median, you are doing better than half of Americans your age. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

Vanguard's annual "How America Saves" report and Fidelity's quarterly retirement analysis provide the most comprehensive snapshots of what Americans hold in their workplace retirement accounts. These numbers reflect defined-contribution plan balances only — primarily 401(k) and 403(b) accounts.

Average balance: $13,265. Median balance: $5,400. Most savers in this bracket have been contributing for fewer than five years. The biggest advantage this group has is time — a 25-year-old contributing $6,000 per year with a 7% average return will accumulate over $1.2 million by age 65 without ever increasing their contribution. The FI community emphasizes that getting started early matters far more than starting with large contributions.

Average balance: $53,300. Median balance: $21,000. This is where employer matches start compounding meaningfully. Fidelity data shows that employees who have been contributing consistently since their 20s have balances 2.5 to 3 times higher than those who started in their 30s. The typical employer match adds 3-6% of salary — effectively free money that many employees still leave on the table. According to Vanguard, roughly 25% of eligible employees do not contribute enough to capture their full employer match.

Average balance: $142,069. Median balance: $60,763. Earnings typically peak in this decade, making it the critical window for aggressive savings. FIRE-path savers in this age bracket commonly have $500,000 to $1 million or more saved by maximizing their 401(k) ($25,500 in 2027), HSA ($4,500 individual / $9,000 family), and Roth IRA ($7,000) — then directing additional savings into taxable brokerage accounts.

Fidelity's guideline of 1x salary by 30 and 10x salary by 67 is a reasonable starting point for traditional retirement planning. But for FI seekers, these benchmarks are the floor, not the ceiling. The ChooseFI community consistently demonstrates that saving 40-60% of income — rather than the national average of 4.6% — compresses the timeline from 40 working years down to 10-17.

If your balance is below the median for your age group, you are not alone — and you are not stuck. The math of compound growth means that aggressive action in your 40s and 50s can still produce a secure retirement or even an early one.

The IRS provides additional contribution room for savers age 50 and older. In 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution is $7,500 on top of the standard $25,500 limit, for a total of $31,000. IRA catch-up contributions add $1,000 to the standard $7,000 limit. HSA catch-up for those 55+ adds another $1,000. Combined with employer matching, a 50-year-old couple can potentially shelter $80,000 or more per year in tax-advantaged accounts.

Most financial advice focuses on investment returns, but the variable you control most directly is your savings rate. Moving from a 10% savings rate to a 30% savings rate has a dramatically larger impact on your retirement timeline than chasing an extra 2% of investment return. A household earning $120,000 that increases from 10% to 30% savings — a shift of $24,000 per year — adds roughly $600,000 to their retirement balance over 15 years (assuming 7% average returns).

The FI community's core insight is that savings rate is the primary driver of financial independence. At a 50% savings rate, you can reach FI in roughly 17 years regardless of income level. At 60%, it compresses to about 12 years. At 70%, you are looking at under 10 years. These numbers are independent of salary — they depend only on the ratio of savings to spending.

The average American contributes 4.6% of salary to their 401(k), receives a 3-4% employer match, and saves little outside of that. FIRE-path savers typically max every available tax-advantaged account, maintain savings rates of 40-60%, invest in low-cost index funds, and direct overflow savings into taxable brokerage accounts. The result: FIRE savers in their 40s commonly have $500,000 to $1.5 million in total investable assets — 5 to 10 times the national median for their age group. The difference is not income; many FIRE success stories come from median-income households that simply saved aggressively and avoided lifestyle inflation.

Roughly one in four employees leaves free employer match money on the table. If your employer matches 50% of contributions up to 6% of salary, you need to contribute at least 6% to capture the full match. This is an instant 50% return on your money — no investment can beat it.

A Roth IRA provides tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals in retirement, with no required minimum distributions. The 2026 limit is $7,000 ($8,000 if 50+). If your income exceeds the Roth limits, use the backdoor Roth conversion strategy to contribute indirectly.

Fidelity recommends having 1x your annual salary saved by age 30. For someone earning $55,000, that means $55,000 in retirement accounts. The FI community targets higher — $50,000 to $100,000 by 30 is common among aggressive savers. The average is pulled upward by a small percentage of very high-balance accounts. If nine people have $10,000 saved and one person has $1,000,000, the average is $109,000 but the median is $10,000. The median gives a far more accurate picture of what a typical American has saved. Always compare yourself to the median, not the average.

Yes — employer matching contributions are part of your retirement savings balance. In a typical arrangement, an employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. On a $75,000 salary, that adds $2,250 per year in free money. Over a 30-year career at 7% returns, that match alone grows to roughly $213,000.

You would need to sell or reverse-mortgage your home to access that equity. Retirement planning should focus on investable assets — accounts you can convert to income without selling your primary residence.

A common guideline is 10-12x your pre-retirement income. For a household earning $100,000, that means $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 in retirement savings. The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually with a high probability of not running out over 30 years — so $1 million supports roughly $40,000 per year in withdrawals.

It is never too late, but the urgency increases with age. A 40-year-old saving $20,000 per year at 7% returns will accumulate roughly $1 million by age 65. A 50-year-old has access to catch-up contributions ($7,500 extra in a 401(k)) and can still build $400,000 to $600,000 in 15 years with aggressive saving. The key is maximizing savings rate immediately rather than trying to make up ground through risky investments.

The average retirement savings benchmarks are useful directional guides, but they should not define your target. Most Americans are dramatically undersaved — the median 401(k) balance at retirement age is under $75,000, which supports only about $2,860 per year in withdrawals using the 4% rule. That is not a retirement plan; it is a supplement to Social Security at best. The FI community takes a fundamentally different approach: define your actual annual spending, multiply by 25, and work backward to a savings rate that gets you there. Whether your number is $750,000 or $3 million, the path is the same — maximize tax-advantaged accounts, invest in low-cost index funds, maintain a high savings rate, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting. If you are behind the benchmarks, the single most impactful action is increasing your savings rate, not chasing higher returns.

#9375. The best Thanksgiving baking tips from Ina Garten, Erin McDowell, and more pro bakers: Top tips from the Things Bakers Know podcast.

It’s the most wonderful baking season of the year, and to help you bake your best, we have top tips from some of the country’s best bakers, pulled from conversations on the Things Bakers Know podcast. Below, you’ll find Thanksgiving strategies from podcast guests Ina Garten, King Arthur’s Martin Philip, Erin McDowell, Helen Goh, and many more of our baking friends.

“The one thing I think people think they can do is multiply a recipe times four and think it’s going to come out fine, which it won’t,” Ina shared on her podcast episode. Instead of taking one recipe and just multiplying by three or four, she suggests either baking the original recipe multiple times, or doubling it and baking two or three times, depending on how many people you’re feeding. Just don’t multiply more than once! If you do, the leavening and flavoring starts to get thrown off.

If you’re baking for a lot of people, Ina also suggests making recipes scaled for a baking sheet. As she explains, “It’s easier to bake, and it’s easier to cut.” We’d recommend Slab Chocolate Pecan Pie, Pumpkin Cake Bars with Cream Cheese Frosting, or Walnut and Oat Slab Pie.

While you may be excited to try out a show-stopping recipe from a brand-new cookbook, Ina recommends resisting temptation. “You don’t want to test something you haven’t made a million times,” she cautions. “Even for me, it adds enormous stress.” Instead of turning to a first-time recipe, Ina highly recommends that you “do the things you know will come out perfectly every time.” And if you do want to make a new-to-you recipe this Thanksgiving, consider baking it once or twice in the weeks leading up to the holiday, so you have the chance to practice and work out any kinks (like figuring out make-ahead components or fridge storage) before hosting on the big day.

No one wants a soggy bottom on their pie, especially a super-juicy one like apple pie. Erin McDowell has lots of tips to avoid a soggy bottom, but her biggest one is to precook your apple filling before assembling your pie. “We can't necessarily predict how juicy any given fruit is, so even if you're using the same apple … each time, they are going to be a little bit different,” she explained on our podcast episode all about apples. Precooking the filling allows you to adjust based on the juiciness of the fruit you’re using that day. “If you're dealing with not-very-juicy apples, you may not have to cook it as long. If they're really juicy, you may have to cook it longer, but the process is the same.”

Pie crust can be incredibly intimidating for some bakers. But pie queen Stacey Mei Yan Fong says the key to success is sometimes to chill out, figuratively and literally. “The best thing you can do is just chill, as in calm down. You're not doing brain surgery,” she reminded Jessica in our Thanksgiving pie episode. “And also use your fridge!” As she points out, “the minute things start getting too wet or things start getting too warm, that's when people panic.” So take a moment to chill the dough and make it easier to work with. If the butter's getting soft or your pie dough is getting difficult to work with, just put it in the fridge to cool down for 10 to 15 minutes.

It’s not just the fridge, either — your freezer can also be incredibly helpful. Stacey likes to freeze her pies before baking, which she says helps the crimping hold its shape as it bakes. And remember that, as Stacey points out, “Pie is kind of a lesson in patience.”

On our special Holiday Q+A Extravaganza, King Arthur’s Director of Baking Education Amber Eisler has a crucial tip for avoiding runny apple pies — make sure you see your pie filling actively bubbling through the vents in your pie crust. As she explains, “It means the filling has boiled and bubbled, so the starches in the filling are actually thickening, which is a super important part of [avoiding a soupy pie].”

There’s a lot of cooking and baking happening around Thanksgiving, which means your oven can get pretty crowded, pretty quickly. But be wary of overfilling it. Even though your oven may have up to three racks inside, Martin Philip cautions against using them all at the same time. “Don’t make the mistake of crowding the oven when it comes to rolls. Let bread have its moment,” he says. Bake your pies the day before to save oven space; a turkey, too will stay hot out of the oven for hours. When baking rolls, you want “top and bottom heat, use your convection setting, make sure that air is moving,” says Martin. “Guard the rolls, y’all!”

Cookbook author and professional psychologist Helen Goh believes in the power of baking to bring meaning and fulfillment to our lives. During this busy holiday season, full of messy kitchens, family squabbles, lengthy to-do lists, and lots of hosting, it can be easy to get overwhelmed. But baking can actually be a calming, comforting activity right now. “Some people say baking makes them nervous because you have to focus,” says Helen. But part of the therapeutic effect of baking comes from forcing us to focus on a single task at hand. As she points out, “that takes you away from all that white noise about what you did yesterday or what's going to happen tomorrow,” and instead allows you to live mindfully in the moment.

Happy Thanksgiving from all of us here at King Arthur. If you run into baking troubles or just need a little support in the kitchen, our Baker’s Hotline is here to help.

#9374. Give Your McDonald's Egg McMuffin Double The Flavor With A Twist Workers Love

McDonald's Egg McMuffin is an iconic sandwich within the fast food breakfast realm. The chain took the McMuffin from good to great when its restaurants began toasting the English muffin halves in real butter rather than margarine. Customers have also found their own methods for upgrading this legendary breakfast sandwich, such as adding hash brown patties into the mix or giving it a flavor twist with sweet add-ons. The latter practice actually harks back to the 1970s, when the sandwich was served with sugary condiments like honey and jam. While that didn't last long as a standard practice, you can still DIY your own sweet toppings to get twice the eating pleasure out of just one Egg McMuffin.

Tristen Epps-Long, Season 22 winner of Bravo's "Top Chef" and a former McDonald's chef, shared this savory-sweet Mickey D's menu hack in an exclusive interview with Food Republic. "I like to take my sandwich apart a little bit, so half of it becomes jellied and buttered and the other half of it becomes open-faced and savory," the expert shared.

Executing this McMuffin double-down is easy to do. Simply remove the sandwich's top English muffin half, exposing the Canadian bacon, egg, and cheese below. This provides the open-faced, savory portion to enjoy — nothing more to do. On the other muffin slice, apply your choice of the Strawberry Preserves or Grape Jam commonly offered at McD's restaurants (or you can combine the two to give your spread a mixed berry vibe). Voila! You have something satisfyingly sweet to crown your McMuffin feasting.

When sweet meets salty, the resulting flavor wizardry is deeply satisfying. There are various other ways to apply this savory-sweet magic and take your McDonald's Egg McMuffin to the next level. Maple-flavored bacon is a popular breakfast staple, and you can bring that vibe to your McMuffin by pouring McDonald's Hotcake Syrup over the sandwich's Canadian bacon and letting it drip over the other elements. The maple-flavored sweetness brings a delightful dimension to the classic sandwich that is lip-smackingly scrumptious and the perfect foil for its salty heartiness.

Adding a packet of Mickey D's honey is another sweetening twist that gives your McMuffin honey ham flair. The honey is actually offered as a dipping sauce option for Chicken McNuggets, but no diehard Golden Arches diner will let that stop them from drizzling it onto a McMuffin for added sweetness.

McDonald's also frequently releases promotional, limited-time sauces, many of which hit those sweet-savory notes with aplomb. Options like Hot Honey Sauce and spicy-sweet Hunter Sauce were among limited-time options that dropped in 2026. You don't have to strictly wait for a limited-edition sauce, though — Mickey D's Sweet 'N Sour Sauce and Creamy Chili McCrispy Strip Dip are on offer year-round to lend sweetness and other flavor dimensions to your Egg McMuffin.

#9373. This $20 Gadget Is My Grandpa’s Secret To Making Big-Batch Potatoes For The Holidays

It looks a little ridiculous, but I can’t stop watching it work.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Growing up, there was one thing I could always count on: If I expressed even a hint of interest in something my grandpa had, I’d have my very own on my doorstep the minute I returned home... and so would every other member of our family. That’s how we became a family full of Rotatos.

If you don’t know what a Rotato is, allow me to introduce you. This rather bare-bones machine will seamlessly peel your potatoes (and other fruits and veggies, too) in just seconds—and the entertainment value is off the charts.

One day while I was visiting my grandparents, I watched my grandfather use his Rotato to peel enough potatoes for a large batch of latkes, then fry up all the peels. His giant batches allowed him to freeze his latkes and enjoy them for months on end. But why spend time peeling all those potatoes yourself when you could whip out a handy gadget that does it all for you?

The Rotato is a mesmerizing device. Sure, it’s a single-use kitchen product, but I could literally watch this baby peel things for hours. Since I first expressed my awe and received one of my very own (along with my parents, sister, and cousins), I’ve tried the Rotato on all kinds of produce.

Mangos? No problem. Apples? Easy as 1-2-3. Any time I’m making a dish that needs something peeled in bulk, the Rotato is my go-to gadget. And my entire family has hopped on board.

Using it reminds me of putting on a record. You simply place your potato (or veggie of choice) on the spike at the bottom of the device, lower the top spike to hold it in place, and position the peeling blade against the top of the potato. Just press the red button, and the machine does the rest, automatically stopping when the cutter arm reaches the bottom.

And once you’ve watched it tackle a potato, it’s hard not to wonder what other fruits and vegetables you can try next.

According to the Rotato’s instruction manual, it can also peel cucumbers, beets, turnips, avocados, eggplants, squash, zucchini, tomatoes, apples, pears, peaches, kiwis, lemons, limes, and oranges—way more than I even imagined. I’ll have to start dreaming up new recipes.

Since discovering the magic of the Rotato, I’ve used it to make mashed potatoes for Friendsgiving, fruit salad, and much more. Sure, it doesn’t get used consistently year-round, but when you’re cooking for a crew, it’s the handiest thing in the kitchen.

#9372. How to turn any bread dough into rolls: Transform your favorite bread loaf into shareable rolls.

So you have a beloved bread recipe that you'd like to turn into fluffy, single-serving rolls, but you don’t know where to start. We’re here to help — let’s get rolling!

Rolls are basically just tiny bread. Which means that, yes, you can technically make a pan of rolls out of any bread dough.

But first, consider the recipe and what type of rolls you're looking to make. If you want soft, fluffy pull-apart rolls (typically baked nestled together in a pan), consider starting with an enriched dough like brioche, milk bread, or challah. If you want crusty, European-style rolls (often baked on sheet trays), start with a leaner dough, such as this pain au levain.

Essentially, the type of bread you start with will determine the type of rolls you make, so plan accordingly.

Turning a bread recipe into rolls is simple: After the dough has had its first rise (otherwise known as its bulk ferment), divide it into small pieces, shape them into rolls, give them a final rise, and bake. The good news is that you don’t need to make any changes to the recipe itself — simply prepare the dough as written and leave it to undergo its first rise.

Once the bread dough has risen, it's time to divide it. Consider: How many rolls do you want, and how large do you want them to be?

Your best bet for even-sized rolls is to grab a calculator and kitchen scale. While you could divide your dough by eye, it’s faster, easier, and more accurate to use the weight measurements, if possible.

For size reference, the pre-bake weight of dinner rolls typically falls between 60g to 80g each. Imagine a 60g roll as the size of a plum when baked, while a baked 80g roll is closer to a Granny Smith apple. Moving up in the ranks are burger buns, which weigh around 100g or so pre-bake.

Here's how much each rolls should weigh before baking:

If you want small-to-medium dinner rolls: 60g to 70g

If you want medium-to-large dinner rolls: 80g to 90g

If you want extra-large dinner rolls or burger buns: 100g to 110g

Let’s say you’re using our Back-of-the-Bag Oatmeal Bread recipe. The total weight of the dough is about 830g. If your first thought is, “I want eight rolls!” you’re going to wind up with eight oat-y burger bun-sized rolls, because 830g divided by eight is just over 100g per roll. That's likely too large if you're looking to make standard dinner rolls.

To ensure you get properly sized rolls, it’s easiest to start by dividing the total weight of the dough by the weight of the size you want your rolls to be, rather than the number of rolls you want. In this case, 830g ÷ 75g = 11 large dinner rolls.

Once divided, it's time to shape the pieces of bread dough. If you’ve never shaped dinner rolls, have no fear! We have you covered, no matter the shape you choose. Basic round rolls? Got it. Fancy shapes? Yep. Braided rolls? You bet. And so much more. Often it helps to see the process in action, especially when it comes to hand positioning when shaping rolls.

For gluten-free breads, scoop the “dough” into a greased muffin pan rather than attempt to shape rolls by hand, since the dough is more like batter. If you're making medium or large gluten-free rolls, check out our Gluten-Free Dinner Rolls recipe for more details.

Small rolls won’t take as long to bake as a loaf would. Most will take around 20 to 30 minutes to bake, depending on their size. You can usually stick with the temperature your original recipe calls for, but 350°F is a safe bet, too.

A final note: Rolls baked close together in "pull-apart" style will usually take a bit longer to bake than they would if they were spaced out on a baking sheet.

And remember, if you make more rolls than you can eat in one sitting, you can always freeze and bake them.

We're diving deep on rolls ahead of Thanksgiving in our latest podcast episode, all about rolls.

#9369. The two-second step to caramelize your pie crust : Just add sugar.

Most pie recipes will instruct you to sprinkle sparkling sugar or turbinado sugar on top of your egg-washed pie crust just before baking, so the coarse sugar can make those edges extra-crunchy and add a bit of glittery sheen. But why stop there — what if the bottom crust got the same treatment too?

That's what our Test Kitchen wondered while developing a new galette recipe for our newest cookbook (coming out next year!). While working on an apricot galette recipe, they tried adding a finishing sugar to the bottom of the dough before baking, and found that it created a crunchy, sugary, caramelized crust that elevated the entire dessert.

As an added bonus, this technique can help ensure a crunchy, well-browned bottom crust;  consider this step another line of defense against a soggy bottom, like baking your pie on a pizza stone or steel or baking pie on the bottom rack of the oven,

You can apply it to any pie (or galette!) recipe while rolling out the dough. Here’s how to do it:

On a lightly floured surface, roll the dough to a 10" to 12" round (aim for the smaller diameter for pie crusts, and larger for galettes). Sprinkle around 1 tablespoon of sparkling sugar or turbinado sugar all over the dough. (It’s important to only use these larger, coarse-grained sugars — we don’t recommend using granulated sugar.) Sprinkle lightly with flour, then continue to roll the dough to reach a 12" to 14" round. Carefully invert the dough round so that the sugared side is on the bottom of the pie pan (to make a single or double crust pie) or parchment paper (to make a galette).

Use this step in classic applications like apple pie where sparkling sugar can cover the entire thing, from top to bottom crust. Or, use it in custard pies like pecan or pumpkin. If you’re going the galette route for Thanksgiving, use it in our Apple Butter Apple Galette or Tiny Apple Tarts for Two. Regardless of the pie you choose, the crust — not the filling! — may be what steals the show.
